tracks.name: Algorithms & Problem Solving
tracks.description:
Developing algorithmic thinking and problem-solving skills: from complexity analysis and fundamental data structures to confidently selecting patterns, solving Medium-level problems, and passing coding interviews.
The focus is not the number of solved problems. It is the ability to independently break down a problem, select appropriate data structures and algorithms, explain solution correctness, evaluate Time/Space Complexity, and handle edge cases.
tracks.resources:
Must:
NeetCode Roadmap / NeetCode 150 — the primary topic order and problem set: https://neetcode.io/roadmap
LeetCode — the main practice platform: https://leetcode.com
Yandex Education, “Algorithm Fundamentals” — theory, exercises, and performance validation: https://education.yandex.ru/handbook/algorithms

Useful:
Aditya Bhargava, “Grokking Algorithms” — intuition for Big O, hash tables, graphs, and recursion. Read selectively and reinforce every chapter with problems.
Blind 75 — a compact interview-readiness problem set: https://neetcode.io/practice/practice/blind75
Big-O Cheat Sheet — a quick complexity reference: https://www.bigocheatsheet.com

Practice rule:
1. Spend 25–30 minutes solving independently.
2. If stuck, study the core idea instead of copying the implementation.
3. Solve the same problem again from a blank file the next day and explain its Time/Space Complexity.
4. Keep notes: pattern, key insight, mistake, and edge case.

Solves simple problems with one or two logical steps without hints. The goal is to stop writing nested loops “just in case” and start recognizing when information should be stored for later lookup.

tracks.name: Code Quality & Maintainability
tracks.description:
Building the skill of writing laconic, explicit, and cheap-to-change code: from names and function shape, through side effects and SOLID, to a refactor or a pattern — and knowing when not to use one.
Quality here means the next change is cheaper and the next reader is not guessing. It is not visual neatness, not one class per principle, and not Clean Architecture or TDD. Those belong in other tracks.
tracks.resources:
Must. Martin Fowler, Refactoring, 2nd ed., JavaScript examples. Catalog, not cover to cover. L3–L4, when a smell needs a small step and behavior stays the same. About 15–20 hours, targeted.
Must. Refactoring Guru, Design Patterns. L4 dictionary only: Adapter, Strategy, Factory, Facade, Observer, Decorator. Skip the other 16 until a real pain shows up. About 6–8 hours. https://refactoring.guru/design-patterns
Must. John Ousterhout, A Philosophy of Software Design, 2nd ed. L5 counterweight to Clean Code: deep modules, cost of abstraction. About 8–12 hours. Skip until L4 is real.
Useful. Robert C. Martin, Clean Code. L1–L2 only: names, functions, error handling. Checklist, not a bible. About 8–12 hours, then two weeks of use in real pull requests.
Optional. Gang of Four cover to cover. Clean Architecture. SOLID video rituals. Any rule that a switch, or a function over N lines, is always wrong.

No new types.

tracks.name: Testing & Test Strategy
tracks.description:
Choosing and writing automated tests that buy confidence without locking the implementation. From a single failing assertion, through the unit and integration boundary, to a small Playwright suite and a reviewable strategy.
The point is not coverage and not the number of tests. It is knowing which bug a test should catch, which layer is the cheapest honest check, and when a test should be deleted because it only freezes the current code.
Scope is Vitest for unit and integration, Testing Library for behavior, MSW at the network boundary, and Playwright for a few real user journeys. Mobile e2e, visual regression as a product, and performance testing stay outside this track. TypeScript and lint are the base of the trophy, but they belong to other tracks.
tracks.resources:
Testing Library Guiding Principles — L2, must. Why a test should resemble use, not internals. Read the principles, then rewrite one bad test. 1–2 h. Skip the query encyclopedia if reviews already catch implementation-detail tests.
Vitest Getting Started — L1–L3, must. Runner, expect, mocks, config. Official guide only. 3–5 h. Skip the advanced API until L4.
Kent C. Dodds, "Write tests. Not too many. Mostly integration." — L3, must. Why UI suites should not be a pile of solitary units. 45 min.
Kent C. Dodds, "The Testing Trophy and Testing Classifications" — L3, must. Shared words for static, unit, integration, and e2e. 45 min. Philosophy, not a tool API.
Ham Vocke, "The Practical Test Pyramid" — L3–L5, must. Layers, contract seams, cost of broad tests. Skip the Java samples. 2–3 h. Skip until L2 is closed.
Playwright Best Practices — L4, must. Isolation, resilient tests, traces. Pair with locators and Trace Viewer. 2–3 h. Skip Electron and extension chapters.
web.dev, "Pyramid or Crab?" — L3–L5, useful. When the pyramid fits and when the trophy fits. 45 min.
MSW docs — L3, useful. One network mock for Vitest and the browser. 2–3 h. Skip until a test hits an API.
Vitest Browser Mode — L4, useful. Real browser when jsdom lies. 2 h. Do not adopt it as a second e2e suite.
Martin Fowler, "Test Pyramid" — L3, useful. Short balance heuristic. 20 min. Skip if the Practical Test Pyramid is already read.

tracks.name: AI-Assisted Engineering
tracks.description:
Using AI coding assistants and agents as a reliable engineering capability: from task framing and context management to agent harnesses, reusable skills, tool integrations, automated verification, and safe delivery.
The focus is not generating more code. It is defining work precisely, providing the right context and constraints, delegating effectively, reviewing every generated change, and remaining accountable for correctness, security, maintainability, and product impact.

tracks.name: System Design & Architecture
tracks.description:
Designing software systems that meet product requirements under real-world constraints: scale, latency, reliability, security, maintainability, operational complexity, and cost.
The focus is not naming infrastructure components. It is clarifying requirements, modeling data and traffic, defining system boundaries and contracts, selecting appropriate trade-offs, and explaining how the system behaves when demand, dependencies, or assumptions fail.

Understands the basic building blocks of a production system and can describe how a user request travels through a client, network, API, application, database, and external dependencies.
Can turn a vague feature request into functional requirements, non-functional requirements, assumptions, and explicit out-of-scope items. Draws a simple component diagram and identifies ownership, boundaries, inputs, outputs, and data flow without introducing distributed systems by default.

Understands when to use caching, asynchronous processing, pagination, rate limiting, CDN delivery, and database indexes. Can distinguish a browser performance issue, an API latency issue, a database query issue, and a network delivery issue.

Selects between synchronous and asynchronous communication, understands replication and partitioning at a practical level, and defines consistency, delivery, retry, timeout, and recovery behavior explicitly. Makes architecture evolutionary: can split or preserve a monolith based on business and team needs, migrate data safely, deprecate contracts, and reduce risk through incremental delivery. Treats security and cost as design constraints from the first diagram.

Reviews designs for hidden coupling, unclear ownership, unmeasured reliability claims, security gaps, scaling assumptions, operational burden, and unnecessary complexity. tracks.name: Modern Layout & Responsive Design
tracks.description: Build resilient, accessible, and component-friendly web layouts that adapt to viewport size, container size, zoom level, content length, user preferences, and input capabilities. Use semantic HTML, intrinsic sizing, modern CSS layout primitives, media and container queries, and progressive enhancement to preserve usability across phones, tablets, desktops, TVs, keyboard-only navigation, touch, mouse, and mixed-input devices.
tracks.resources:
MUST — MDN: Responsive design. L1–L3. Official foundation for responsive layouts, viewport configuration, flexible media, and media queries. Read once, then rebuild each example without copying. 2–3 hours. Skip only if you can already explain why device-specific breakpoints are fragile. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Learn_web_development/Core/CSS_layout/Responsive_Design
MUST — web.dev: Responsive web design basics. L1–L4. A practical mobile-first view of fluid layouts, responsive images, viewport behavior, and interaction modes. Use it as a checklist while building the L2 project. 1–2 hours. https://web.dev/articles/responsive-web-design-basics
MUST — MDN: CSS Container Queries. L3–L5. Learn component-level responsiveness: container types, size queries, container query units, and when viewport queries are the wrong abstraction. Build the L4 component set alongside it. 2–3 hours. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/Guides/Containment/Container_queries
MUST — W3C: Media Queries Level 5. L4–L5. Primary specification for hover, pointer, any-hover, any-pointer, prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-contrast, and other environment queries. Read selected sections, not cover to cover. 2–4 hours. https://www.w3.org/TR/mediaqueries-5/
USE AS ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA — WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 1.4.10 Reflow. L2–L5. Test at 320 CSS px and 400% browser zoom; do not accept horizontal scrolling caused by ordinary page content. 30–45 minutes. https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/#reflow
PRACTICE — Every Layout. L2–L4. Recreate real responsive layouts with CSS Grid and Flexbox, then compare your solution to the reference. Complete 8–12 challenges; avoid treating a screenshot-perfect desktop result as done. 8–15 hours. https://every-layout.dev/
USEFUL — Kevin Powell: Conquering Responsive Layouts. L1–L3. A guided practical course for fluid CSS, responsive typography, and layout debugging. Take it if the CSS fundamentals feel mechanical rather than intuitive. 21 days, 20–30 minutes per day. https://courses.kevinpowell.co/conquering-responsive-layouts

levels.description: Design reusable components that adapt to the space and context in which they are placed. Use container queries when a component should respond to its parent rather than the global viewport, and define clear layout contracts for component consumers.

Provide touch targets and spacing that remain usable with coarse pointers.
Use prefers-reduced-motion to remove or reduce non-essential animation without removing feedback or state changes.
Support prefers-color-scheme and prefers-contrast without creating inaccessible color combinations.
Test a responsive menu using keyboard only, touch emulation, mouse, and a device with both touch and mouse input.
Exit criterion: Review an interface for interaction assumptions and fix every feature that depends exclusively on hover, precise pointing, or a fixed viewport.

levels.name: Resilient Layout Systems and Debugging
levels.description: Design and review a production-ready responsive layout system. Diagnose complex overflow, sizing, rendering, and cross-device issues; establish tokens and test matrices; and make deliberate trade-offs between visual fidelity, maintainability, accessibility, and performance.
examples: Debug overflow caused by intrinsic minimum sizes, flex items, grid tracks, replaced elements, transforms, and long unbreakable content.
Explain when min-width: 0, overflow-wrap: anywhere, overflow: clip, contain, content-visibility, and aspect-ratio are appropriate or dangerous.
Create a responsive token system for spacing, typography, page gutters, content widths, grid gaps, and component breakpoints.
Audit a production page with browser DevTools device emulation, responsive mode, zoom, forced colors, reduced motion, print mode, and real-device testing.
Set up visual regression coverage for representative viewports, content lengths, themes, and interaction modes.
Review a pull request for layout resilience, accessibility reflow, input assumptions, and unnecessary breakpoint duplication.
Explain trade-offs between a single fluid layout, viewport breakpoints, container queries, separate component variants, and server-selected markup.
Exit criterion: Lead a layout-system review, identify root causes instead of patching symptoms, and leave behind reusable rules, tokens, and regression tests.

tracks.name: TypeScript & JavaScript Runtime
tracks.description: Understand how JavaScript executes in the browser: ECMAScript semantics, scope, closures, prototypes, execution contexts, tasks, microtasks, rendering opportunities, browser APIs, memory management, and V8 optimization behavior. Use TypeScript as a pragmatic tool for explicit domain models, safe boundaries, and readable code. Prefer simple object types, unions, narrowing, and composition over clever type-level programming or inheritance-heavy class hierarchies.
tracks.resources:
MUST — MDN: JavaScript execution model. L1–L3. Official mental model for execution contexts, call stack, jobs, event loop, tasks, and microtasks. Read carefully, then manually predict output for every asynchronous example before running it. 2–3 hours. Do not skip. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/JavaScript/Reference/Execution_model
MUST — MDN: Using microtasks with queueMicrotask(). L2–L4. Precise browser-oriented explanation of task and microtask ordering, rendering opportunities, Promise callbacks, and microtask starvation. Recreate every ordering example in DevTools. 1–2 hours. Do not skip. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/HTML_DOM_API/Microtask_guide
MUST — TypeScript Handbook: Everyday Types, Narrowing, Object Types, and Classes. L1–L3. Learn the small, high-leverage TypeScript subset for production frontend: primitives, object types, unions, optional properties, narrowing, discriminated unions, interfaces, and classes. Read in this order; avoid advanced utility and conditional types until a real codebase requirement appears. 6–10 hours. https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/everyday-types.html
https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html
https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html
https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/classes.html
MUST — Chrome DevTools: Analyze runtime performance. L3–L5. Learn to record, read, and validate a Performance profile instead of guessing about JavaScript speed. Use it for every L4 and L5 optimization exercise. 2–4 hours plus practice. Do not skip. https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/performance
MUST — Chrome DevTools: Fix memory problems. L4–L5. Practical workflow for distinguishing memory leaks, memory bloat, and frequent garbage collection with heap snapshots and allocation timelines. 2–3 hours. Skip only until you own a long-lived browser feature. https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/memory-problems
USEFUL — V8: Fast properties. L4–L5. Primary V8 article on hidden classes, property shapes, and inline caches. Read after profiling basics; use it to interpret evidence, not to cargo-cult object construction rules. 1–2 hours. https://v8.dev/blog/fast-properties
USEFUL — V8: Trash talk: the Orinoco garbage collector. L5. Primary overview of V8 garbage collection and concurrent, parallel, and incremental collection work. Read for runtime intuition, not API-level tuning recipes. 1–2 hours. https://v8.dev/blog/trash-talk
REFERENCE — ECMAScript Language Specification. L3–L5. Use as a targeted reference for execution contexts, jobs, Promise resolution, iterators, and language edge cases. Never attempt to read it linearly. 30–90 minutes per investigation. https://tc39.es/ecma262/

levels.name: JavaScript and TypeScript Foundations
levels.description: Write predictable JavaScript using values, objects, arrays, functions, scope, closures, modules, and prototypes. Model everyday application data in TypeScript with explicit and readable types. Understand that TypeScript validates source code but does not change JavaScript runtime behavior.
examples: Explain primitives, reference values, equality, mutation, shallow copying, and why const does not make an object immutable.
Predict the result of code using lexical scope, block scope, function scope, closures, this, and arrow functions.
Explain prototype lookup and the relationship between constructor functions, class syntax, instances, and Object.prototype.
Build a small state module with ES modules, closures, immutable updates, and a public API.
Define simple object types, arrays, function signatures, optional properties, and nullable values without using any.
Use unknown at an untrusted boundary and narrow it before use.
Model one UI state with a discriminated union instead of multiple independent boolean flags.
Explain why TypeScript types disappear after compilation and cannot validate server responses at runtime.
Exit criterion: Implement a small browser feature in strict TypeScript with zero explicit any types and explain its JavaScript runtime behavior.

levels.name: Async Execution and Browser Event Loop
levels.description: Explain how synchronous code, browser APIs, tasks, microtasks, Promises, async functions, timers, events, and rendering opportunities interact. Predict execution order from code and choose scheduling primitives deliberately.
examples: Draw the call stack, browser API boundary, task queue, microtask queue, and rendering opportunity for a user interaction.
Predict output order for synchronous code, setTimeout(), Promise.then(), queueMicrotask(), async and await, and DOM events.
Explain why await does not block the browser thread but does split an async function into later Promise-based work.
Implement a debounced search input, a throttled scroll handler, and a cancellable request flow using AbortController.
Demonstrate microtask starvation by recursively scheduling queueMicrotask() and explain why rendering is delayed.
Use requestAnimationFrame for visual updates and explain why it differs from setTimeout().
Identify an accidental long task in a browser trace and split or defer work without changing visible behavior.
Exit criterion: Correctly solve ten event-loop ordering exercises and diagnose one interaction delay with the Performance panel.

levels.name: Runtime Semantics and Safe Domain Modeling
levels.description: Reason about advanced JavaScript behavior at application boundaries: property access, descriptors, iterables, errors, async failures, modules, and object identity. Model domain states with simple TypeScript constructs and choose composition over class inheritance by default.
examples: Explain property lookup, own versus inherited properties, getters, setters, descriptors, and the practical risks of prototype mutation.
Use Map, Set, WeakMap, and WeakSet appropriately and explain their identity and garbage-collection implications.
Implement custom error classes and preserve useful error context across an asynchronous boundary.
Design a runtime validation boundary for unknown API data and return a typed success or failure result.
Model a payment, upload, or form workflow with discriminated unions and exhaustive switch checking.
Use type guards, assertion functions, generics with meaningful constraints, and readonly only where they improve a real API.
Implement a class only when it represents behavior plus encapsulated state; use interfaces and composition instead of inheritance for feature reuse.
Explain structural typing, excess property checks, type erasure, and the difference between compile-time safety and runtime validation.
Exit criterion: Refactor a confusing any-based feature into a readable domain model with runtime validation and no inheritance hierarchy deeper than one level.

levels.name: V8, Memory, and Evidence-Based Performance
levels.description: Use browser profiling tools to locate JavaScript CPU and memory problems, form a measurable hypothesis, and verify an improvement. Understand V8 concepts such as object shapes, inline caches, tiered execution, deoptimization, and garbage collection well enough to avoid harmful code patterns without premature micro-optimization.
examples: Record a Performance trace for a slow interaction and identify scripting, rendering, layout, paint, idle time, and long tasks.
Explain why a long task over 50 milliseconds harms responsiveness and identify the exact function or call path causing it.
Use Performance.mark(), Performance.measure(), console.profile(), and the DevTools Performance panel to compare before and after measurements.
Create a deliberate memory leak through a retained DOM node, event listener, timer, or closure and locate its retaining path in a heap snapshot.
Differentiate a memory leak, memory bloat, normal allocation churn, and garbage-collection activity using evidence.
Explain hidden classes and inline caches as V8 implementation mechanisms, including why stable object shapes can help property access.
Identify optimization folklore that is not supported by a production profile and remove the unnecessary complexity.
Exit criterion: Produce a short performance investigation with a reproducible scenario, trace or heap evidence, a targeted fix, and measured before-and-after results.

levels.name: Runtime Architecture and Technical Review
levels.description: Set JavaScript and TypeScript runtime conventions for a frontend system. Review asynchronous flows, type boundaries, memory ownership, and performance decisions; teach the execution model; and prevent regressions through observability, tests, and architecture.
examples: Define team rules for strict TypeScript, forbidden any usage, unknown boundaries, runtime schemas, assertion policy, and intentionally accepted escapes.
Review an asynchronous feature for cancellation, race conditions, stale responses, unhandled rejections, resource cleanup, and user-visible loading states.
Design a data-fetching or background-processing flow that remains correct when a component unmounts, a request is superseded, or the network is slow.
Establish a performance debugging playbook based on reproduction, measurement, hypothesis, minimal change, verification, and regression protection.
Review a pull request and distinguish measurable runtime concerns from speculative V8 micro-optimizations.
Set a profiling test matrix for low-end CPU throttling, memory pressure, slow network, large data sets, frequent interactions, and long-lived sessions.
Teach a developer to predict event-loop behavior and verify it with a minimal DevTools experiment.
Exit criterion: Lead a runtime incident or performance review and leave behind an actionable guideline, a reproducible test case, and a regression safeguard.

tracks.name: Browser & APIs
tracks.description: Use the browser as an application platform. Understand the critical rendering path, page lifecycle, network and caching behavior, storage, browser communication, background work, and real-time transport. Select native Web APIs based on the problem, verify compatibility and lifecycle constraints, handle cancellation and cleanup, and measure rendering and network effects with browser DevTools.
tracks.resources:
MUST — web.dev: Understand the critical path. L1–L3. Primary practical overview of how HTML, CSS, JavaScript, DOM, CSSOM, render tree, style, layout, paint, and compositing produce visible pixels. Read once, then reproduce the pipeline in Performance DevTools. 1–2 hours. Do not skip. https://web.dev/learn/performance/understanding-the-critical-path

MUST — web.dev: Rendering performance. L1–L4. Practical explanation of the pixel pipeline and how JavaScript and CSS changes can trigger style recalculation, layout, paint, or compositing. Use it while running L2 rendering experiments. 2–3 hours. https://web.dev/articles/rendering-performance

MUST — MDN: Fetch API and AbortController. L1–L3. Build resilient browser network calls with Request, Response, headers, body parsing, errors, cancellation, and AbortSignal. Use this instead of treating fetch as a one-line JSON helper. 2–4 hours. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Fetch_API
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/AbortController

MUST — MDN: HTTP caching and Cache-Control. L2–L4. Learn browser and shared-cache behavior, freshness, validation, Cache-Control, ETag, Last-Modified, and why the server defines most HTTP cache policy. 2–3 hours. Do not skip. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching
https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Cache-Control

MUST — Chrome DevTools: Network features reference. L2–L5. Learn to inspect requests, headers, timing, initiators, response bodies, caching, throttling, request blocking, and overrides. Use it during every network-related exercise. 2–4 hours plus continuous practice. https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/network/reference

MUST — MDN: Service Worker API. L3–L5. Primary reference for service-worker lifecycle, scope, controlled clients, request interception, Cache API, offline behavior, and updates. Read only after HTTP caching fundamentals. 3–5 hours. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Service_Worker_API

USEFUL — MDN: Streams API. L3–L4. Learn when incremental response processing and backpressure matter, such as progressive AI output, large file processing, and media or event data. Build one streaming UI experiment. 2–3 hours. Skip until a real incremental-data use case exists. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Streams_API

USEFUL — MDN: Broadcast Channel API. L3–L4. Use same-origin tab, iframe, and worker communication when localStorage events or server roundtrips would be the wrong tool. 30–60 minutes. Skip until multi-tab coordination is needed. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Broadcast_Channel_API

USEFUL — web.dev: Optimize long tasks. L3–L5. Learn how to locate and split main-thread work and when moving computation off the main thread is justified. 1–2 hours. https://web.dev/articles/optimize-long-tasks

levels.name: Browser Platform Fundamentals
levels.description: Understand the browser as a host environment for JavaScript and recognize the main categories of Web APIs. Build reliable network and storage interactions with explicit error handling, cancellation, cleanup, and user-visible states.
examples: Explain the boundary between ECMAScript, browser-provided Web APIs, browser DevTools, and application framework abstractions.
Classify a requirement as a rendering, network, storage, device capability, background work, communication, or media problem.
Use fetch with method, headers, request body, response status checking, JSON parsing, and meaningful error handling.
Use AbortController to cancel an obsolete fetch request when a component unmounts, a search query changes, or a user explicitly cancels an operation.
Explain why fetch resolves for an HTTP 404 or 500 response and implement explicit response.ok handling.
Store a small user preference with localStorage and explain its synchronous behavior, origin scope, capacity limitations, and privacy implications.
Use sessionStorage for tab-scoped temporary state and explain when it is preferable to localStorage.
Use the Permissions API and feature detection to progressively enable an optional browser capability.
Exit criterion: Build a search or form flow with loading, success, empty, error, cancellation, and cleanup states without a third-party HTTP client.

levels.name: Rendering, Networking, and Client Caching
levels.description: Explain how browser loading, rendering, and network caching affect user-visible performance. Use DevTools evidence to avoid render-blocking work, unnecessary requests, layout thrashing, and accidental cache misses.
examples: Draw the path from HTML response to DOM, CSSOM, render tree, style calculation, layout, paint, compositing, and pixels on screen.
Explain which operations are likely to trigger style recalculation, layout, paint, or compositing and verify the answer in a Performance recording.
Create a forced synchronous layout example by mixing DOM writes and layout reads, then batch work to remove the layout thrashing.
Use requestAnimationFrame for a visual update and explain why it is synchronized with the browser rendering cycle.
Inspect request URL, method, payload, status, headers, initiator, timing, priority, and response in the Network panel.
Explain freshness caching versus validation caching and the roles of Cache-Control, max-age, ETag, If-None-Match, and 304 Not Modified.
Test a versioned static asset with a long cache lifetime and a frequently changing API response with revalidation.
Simulate slow network and CPU throttling, then identify the request or main-thread work delaying visible content.
Exit criterion: Audit one page in DevTools and produce an evidence-based explanation of its render path, slowest request, and cache behavior.

levels.name: Native APIs for Real Application Needs
levels.description: Select and combine browser APIs to solve common product requirements: visibility-aware loading, persistent client data, file access, cross-context communication, background computation, and incremental network processing.
examples: Use IntersectionObserver to implement lazy loading, visibility analytics, or infinite scrolling without scroll-event polling.
Use ResizeObserver to react to element size changes and avoid feedback loops or unnecessary layout work.
Choose between cookies, localStorage, sessionStorage, IndexedDB, Cache API, and in-memory state based on data size, lifetime, offline needs, sensitivity, and access pattern.
Build a file upload flow with File, Blob, FormData, progress feedback where available, cancellation, retry, and object URL cleanup.
Use URL, URLSearchParams, History API, and popstate to synchronize a filter or search state with a shareable URL.
Use BroadcastChannel to synchronize logout, theme changes, draft updates, or cache invalidation across same-origin tabs.
Use a Web Worker for a CPU-bound task and communicate through message passing without assuming DOM access inside the worker.
Render a fetch response incrementally using ReadableStream only when progressive processing materially improves the user experience.
Exit criterion: Implement a small browser-native feature using at least three appropriate APIs and document why simpler alternatives were rejected.

levels.name: Offline, Background, and Real-Time Systems
levels.description: Build resilient browser features that remain useful through unreliable connectivity, multiple tabs, application updates, and real-time server events. Understand the lifecycle and operational risks of Service Workers and persistent client-side state.
examples: Explain the Service Worker lifecycle: registration, install, waiting, activation, control, update, and scope.
Build an offline-first read-only screen using a Service Worker and Cache API while keeping cache versioning and update behavior explicit.
Compare cache-first, network-first, stale-while-revalidate, and network-only strategies and choose one based on freshness, availability, and failure cost.
Explain why Service Workers require HTTPS and why they should not be added merely to cache everything.
Design a safe update prompt or reload strategy that avoids mixing old JavaScript with new HTML and assets.
Use IndexedDB for persistent structured data and define migrations, quota-failure behavior, and recovery paths.
Implement server-driven real-time updates with WebSocket or Server-Sent Events, including reconnect, backoff, stale-state handling, and explicit cleanup.
Coordinate a multi-tab application so duplicate requests, logout, offline queues, and conflicting local state have defined behavior.
Exit criterion: Deliver a small offline or real-time feature with documented caching policy, lifecycle behavior, failure modes, and a manual test plan.

levels.name: Browser Systems Design and Diagnostics
levels.description: Design and review browser-platform architecture for a production frontend. Diagnose cross-layer issues spanning rendering, network, storage, workers, caching, lifecycle, and compatibility; make deliberate trade-offs; and establish team conventions and observability.
examples: Investigate a real user-facing issue by separating server latency, network transfer, client parsing, JavaScript execution, rendering work, cache behavior, and third-party impact.
Create a browser capability strategy using feature detection, progressive enhancement, compatibility data, fallbacks, and telemetry instead of browser user-agent sniffing.
Review a feature for memory cleanup, aborted work, stale events, dangling observers, object URL revocation, worker termination, and WebSocket teardown.
Create an API selection decision record that compares native platform options, framework abstractions, and third-party libraries by capability, reliability, bundle cost, support, and maintenance.
Define a client caching policy covering static assets, HTML, API reads, mutations, user-specific data, sensitive data, invalidation, and offline behavior.
Create a debugging playbook for Network, Performance, Application, Memory, and Rendering DevTools panels.
Profile a long task, split or defer its work, move appropriate CPU-heavy work to a worker, and verify that the interaction becomes responsive.
Teach a teammate to trace a UI symptom back to the responsible browser subsystem instead of applying an unmeasured workaround.
Exit criterion: Lead a browser-platform design or incident review and leave a measured fix, a compatibility strategy, a regression test, and a reusable engineering guideline.

tracks.name: Web Accessibility (a11y)
tracks.description: Build inclusive, compliant, and barrier-free web experiences for everyone. Ground interfaces in semantic HTML, the POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust), and WCAG 2.2 Level AA requirements. Master predictable keyboard navigation, focus management, color contrast, and assistive technology compatibility via WAI-ARIA and the accessibility tree. Combine automated linters with manual keyboard and screen-reader testing to deliver usable experiences across diverse physical abilities, devices, and assistive technologies.
tracks.resources:
MUST — web.dev: Learn Accessibility. L1–L3. Structured, evergreen foundational guide covering semantic HTML, document structure, color contrast, keyboard interaction, and assistive technology. Read through and complete the hands-on audits. 6–8 hours. https://web.dev/learn/accessibility

MUST — W3C: WCAG 2.2 Quick Reference (How to Meet WCAG). L2–L5. The official reference manual filtered by Level A and AA. Use as the authoritative acceptance criteria checklist for contrast, reflow, focus appearance, target sizes, and error identification. 3–5 hours across exercises. https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/quickref/

MUST — W3C: WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG). L3–L5. The definitive pattern catalog for complex accessible widgets (dialogs, accordions, comboboxes, tabs, menus). Follow each pattern's exact keyboard interaction contracts and state attributes. 4–6 hours plus per-widget reference. https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/

MUST — Deque University / axe DevTools: Automated and Manual Accessibility Testing. L2–L4. Learn what automated tools (axe-core, Lighthouse) can catch (roughly 30-50% of defects) and how to conduct manual keyboard and screen-reader passes. 2–3 hours. https://www.deque.com/axe/devtools/

PRACTICE — WebAIM Screen Reader Keyboard Shortcuts and Testing Guides (NVDA, VoiceOver). L3–L5. Master realistic navigation workflows using desktop and mobile screen readers rather than relying exclusively on visual inspection. 3–4 hours of active practice. https://webaim.org/resources/shortcuts/nvda

levels.name: Semantic HTML and Perceivable Content
levels.description: Build pages using valid, semantic HTML elements so meaning, structure, and text alternatives are natively exposed to the browser and assistive technologies without custom scripting. Ensure core content meets contrast and magnification requirements.
examples: Use native landmark elements (<header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, <footer>) and a logical heading hierarchy (h1 through h6) without skipping levels.
Provide meaningful alt text for informative images and mark purely decorative images with empty alt="" or presentation roles.
Label every form control explicitly with <label for="...">, <fieldset>, and <legend> instead of relying on placeholder attributes.
Verify color contrast ratios meet WCAG AA standards (at least 4.5:1 for normal text, 3:1 for large text and UI component borders).
Ensure information is not conveyed solely through color, shape, or sound.
Support text resizing up to 200% and page zooming up to 400% without clipped content or horizontal scrolling on plain text.
Explain why a native <button> or <a> tag should always be chosen over a styled <div> or <span> with a click handler.
Exit criterion: Build an informational multi-section page and form with zero axe-core semantic violations and valid headings and labels.

levels.name: Keyboard Navigation and Focus Management
levels.description: Ensure all interactive elements can be operated completely via keyboard alone. Maintain an uninterrupted, logical tab order, design visible focus states, and prevent keyboard traps.
examples: Navigate the entire page using only Tab, Shift+Tab, Enter, Space, and Esc, confirming that every interactive element is reachable and operable.
Implement clear, high-contrast :focus-visible indicators and explain why outline: none without a replacement is an accessibility defect.
Provide a functional "Skip to main content" link that appears on keyboard focus and moves programmatic focus past repeated headers.
Ensure DOM source order matches visual reading order so keyboard navigation remains predictable.
Explain the difference between tabindex="0" (insert into natural tab order), tabindex="-1" (programmatically focusable only), and positive tabindex (anti-pattern).
Verify that custom interactive widgets do not trap keyboard focus unless intentionally containing focus within a modal dialog.
Ensure click-like event handlers on custom elements also listen for appropriate keypresses (Enter, Space).
Exit criterion: Complete a core user workflow (e.g., browse, fill out form, submit) using solely a physical keyboard with clear focus visibility at every step.

levels.name: WAI-ARIA and Accessible State Modeling
levels.description: Apply WAI-ARIA roles, states, and properties intentionally to convey dynamic changes and custom component semantics that native HTML cannot represent. Follow the First Rule of ARIA and keep programmatic state strictly synchronized with DOM state.
examples: Explain the First Rule of ARIA: do not use ARIA when a native semantic HTML element or attribute already exists.
Expose dynamic component states using aria-expanded, aria-selected, aria-checked, aria-disabled, and aria-hidden.
Connect labels and helper text to controls using aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, and aria-errormessage.
Build an accessible modal dialog: trap focus inside while open, set initial focus, dismiss on Esc, and restore focus to the trigger element on close.
Implement accessible accordion and disclosure patterns following WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide (APG) conventions.
Use aria-live regions (polite vs. assertive) sparingly to notify assistive technologies of asynchronous status changes, toast alerts, or errors.
Inspect the browser's Accessibility Tree in Chrome or Firefox DevTools to verify computed accessible names and roles.
Exit criterion: Implement an accessible modal dialog and tab list according to APG specifications and verify correct name/role/state in the Accessibility Tree.

levels.name: Assistive Technology Testing and Input Diversity
levels.description: Test, audit, and validate interfaces using realistic assistive technologies, including desktop and mobile screen readers, high-contrast modes, and alternative input devices. Support users with motor, cognitive, and sensory variations.
examples: Perform end-to-end testing of a complex user journey using NVDA on Windows or VoiceOver on macOS/iOS.
Audit forms for clear inline error validation, descriptive error messages, and immediate programmatic focus on the first erroneous field.
Ensure interactive targets satisfy minimum target size requirements (at least 24x24 CSS px, preferably 44x44 CSS px) with adequate spacing for touch users.
Support Windows High Contrast Mode / Forced Colors Mode by ensuring borders, icons, and text remain visible using system color keywords.
Respect prefers-reduced-motion by disabling non-essential transitions, parallax scrolling, and autoplaying media that can trigger vestibular disorders.
Avoid content that flashes or blinks more than three times per second to prevent triggering photosensitive seizures.
Combine automated audits (axe-core, Lighthouse) with manual assistive tech testing, identifying why automated scanners miss semantic and operational bugs.
Exit criterion: Conduct a full manual screen-reader and keyboard audit on a multi-step checkout or registration flow and document all identified barriers.

levels.name: Accessibility Systems, Compliance, and Culture
levels.description: Establish an organizational accessibility strategy. Define design system a11y contracts, embed automated checks into CI/CD pipelines, lead WCAG 2.2 AA audits, produce VPAT/ACR compliance artifacts, and educate teams to prevent accessibility regressions.
examples: Integrate automated accessibility checks into unit, integration, and E2E test suites (e.g., vitest-axe, @axe-core/playwright) to prevent regressions in pull requests.
Author accessibility requirements and component contracts for design system primitives (focus styles, tokens, ARIA guidelines, keyboard shortcuts).
Conduct a comprehensive WCAG 2.2 Level AA compliance audit across an entire product and prioritize remediation based on user impact.
Produce or evaluate a Voluntary Product Accessibility Template (VPAT) / Accessibility Conformance Report (ACR).
Establish team governance: define Definition of Done criteria for a11y, conduct inclusive design reviews with designers, and run user testing with disabled individuals.
Review third-party libraries and UI components for accessibility compliance before approving adoption into the tech stack.
Mentor engineers on distinguishing cosmetic accessibility patches from genuine architectural accessibility solutions.
Exit criterion: Establish an automated CI accessibility gate and publish an a11y baseline audit with remediation roadmap for your team's application.

tracks.name: Web Security & Privacy
tracks.description: Safeguard modern web applications and protect user privacy across client-side execution, storage, and network transport. Master browser security mechanisms including the Same-Origin Policy, Content Security Policy (CSP), CORS, Subresource Integrity (SRI), and secure cookie configurations (HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite). Mitigate critical web vulnerabilities such as Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), clickjacking, open redirects, and client-side supply chain attacks. Enforce user privacy by controlling PII leakage, handling storage partitioning, managing consent, and restricting third-party tracking scripts.
tracks.resources:
MUST — OWASP: Top 10 Web Application Security Risks & Client-Side Risks. L1–L4. Authoritative classification of injection (XSS), broken access control, security misconfigurations, and client-side risks like Magecart and sensitive data in storage. Read through the primary risk sheets. 4–6 hours. https://owasp.org/Top10/ and https://owasp.org/projects/top-10-client-side-security-risks/

MUST — MDN: Content Security Policy (CSP). L2–L4. The browser's primary defense-in-depth against XSS, data injection, and malicious frame embedding. Learn directives (default-src, script-src, object-src, frame-ancestors, connect-src), nonce/hash workflows, and report-only mode. 3–4 hours. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CSP

MUST — MDN: HTTP Cookies, SameSite, and Secure Contexts. L1–L3. Master HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite (Strict, Lax, None) cookies to safeguard authentication credentials against XSS theft and CSRF exploits. 2–3 hours. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Reference/Headers/Set-Cookie

MUST — PortSwigger Web Security Academy: Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) & CSRF Labs. L2–L4. Interactive browser security labs to exploit and patch DOM-based XSS, reflected XSS, and CSRF vulnerabilities in realistic scenarios. 6–10 hours of hands-on practice. https://portswigger.net/web-security

USEFUL — web.dev & Privacy Sandbox: Third-Party Cookie Restrictions and Storage Partitioning. L3–L5. Understand modern browser privacy primitives: CHIPS (Cookies Having Independent Partitioned State), Storage Access API, and sandboxed iframes. 2–3 hours. https://privacysandbox.google.com/cookies

USEFUL — W3C / MDN: Permissions Policy (Feature Policy). L3–L5. Restrict sensitive browser APIs (camera, microphone, geolocation, screen sharing, payment) in your document and embedded third-party iframes. 1–2 hours. https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Permissions-Policy

levels.name: Web Security Fundamentals and Safe Storage
levels.description: Understand the browser security boundary: the Same-Origin Policy (SOP), HTTPS encryption, and safe client storage. Prevent basic data leakage by keeping authentication secrets out of vulnerable browser storage mechanisms.
examples: Define the Same-Origin Policy (protocol, host, port) and explain what it allows and what it strictly isolates.
Explain why sensitive authentication tokens or credentials must never be stored in localStorage or sessionStorage due to universal script accessibility.
Configure session cookies with HttpOnly (prevents JavaScript access), Secure (HTTPS only), and SameSite=Lax/Strict (mitigates CSRF). [96][103]
Demonstrate how an unescaped DOM insertion via innerHTML or dangerouslySetInnerHTML creates a Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability.
Identify why client-side authorization checks (e.g., hiding an admin button in UI) are strictly cosmetic and do not substitute for server-side verification.
Sanitize user-provided HTML using standard browser APIs or battle-tested libraries (such as DOMPurify) before injecting it into the DOM.
Verify that all application assets, APIs, and external fonts/scripts are exclusively requested over secure HTTPS contexts.
Exit criterion: Secure a client-side login session using HttpOnly cookies with zero secrets exposed to window.localStorage.

levels.name: Attack Vectors: XSS, CSRF, and Clickjacking
levels.description: Identify, explain, and mitigate core web attack vectors: Reflected, Stored, and DOM-based XSS, Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF), clickjacking, and open redirects.
examples: Distinguish between Stored, Reflected, and DOM-based XSS, identifying sinks such as eval(), document.write(), location.href, and innerHTML.
Trace a DOM-based XSS vulnerability from an untrusted source (such as location.hash, searchParams, or postMessage) into an unsafe execution sink.
Explain how SameSite cookies, custom request headers (e.g., X-Requested-With), and anti-CSRF tokens prevent Cross-Site Request Forgery.
Prevent clickjacking attacks using the HTTP frame-ancestors CSP directive or X-Frame-Options: DENY / SAMEORIGIN.
Audit client-side URL redirects to ensure user input cannot redirect to external attacker-controlled origins (javascript: URIs or open redirects).
Validate origin and source before handling window.postMessage events received from third-party iframes or popups.
Inspect HTTP response security headers in DevTools (Strict-Transport-Security, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff).
Exit criterion: Identify and remediate one simulated DOM-based XSS vulnerability and one CSRF vulnerability in a working web application.

levels.name: Defensive Headers, CSP, and Supply Chain Integrity
levels.description: Deploy defense-in-depth mechanisms via HTTP response headers. Configure strict Content Security Policies (CSP), lock down cross-origin resources with CORS, and verify third-party script integrity using Subresource Integrity (SRI).
examples: Design and deploy a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) with default-src 'self', script-src with nonces or hashes, and no 'unsafe-inline' or 'unsafe-eval'. [94]
Implement CSP in Report-Only mode (Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only) with a report-to / report-uri collector before enforcing it in production.
Configure Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) correctly, explaining why Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * with credentials enabled is invalid and dangerous.
Protect externally hosted CDN scripts (e.g., analytics, widgets) using Subresource Integrity (SRI) hashes (integrity="sha384-...") and crossorigin="anonymous".
Audit package dependencies for known CVEs using npm audit or lockfile scanners and eliminate unmaintained third-party packages.
Isolate untrusted embedded third-party widgets using `<iframe sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms">` to restrict parent document access.
Use Permissions-Policy to explicitly disallow unnecessary browser capabilities (camera, microphone, geolocation) for third-party embeds.
Exit criterion: Deploy an enforced CSP with nonces on a multi-page app with zero console violations and no 'unsafe-inline'.

levels.name: Privacy Engineering, Consent, and Third-Party Isolation
levels.description: Architect web applications that respect user privacy, comply with data protection principles, and remain resilient in an era of third-party cookie phase-outs, browser tracking protections, and storage partitioning.
examples: Audit an application's outgoing network traffic to identify PII (email, names, phone numbers) accidentally leaked to third-party tracking pixels or error monitoring tools (e.g., Sentry).
Sanitize telemetry payloads and URL query parameters to ensure session identifiers, passwords, and sensitive search terms are not transmitted.
Implement cookie and tracking consent workflows that defer loading analytics, marketing scripts, and pixels until explicit user opt-in is granted.
Adapt application authentication and embedding flows to browser storage partitioning and third-party cookie restrictions (using CHIPS or the Storage Access API). [95][99]
Configure Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin to prevent leaking sensitive path parameters in HTTP Referer headers.
Use Chrome/Safari private windows and tracking prevention modes to test application functionality when third-party storage is completely disabled.
Detect and prevent client-side JavaScript supply chain skimming attacks (e.g., Magecart style keyloggers injected into payment fields). [100][105]
Exit criterion: Conduct a full data-privacy audit on checkout/form flows, ensuring zero PII leaks to third-party endpoints and clean consent-gated script loading.

levels.name: Security Governance, Threat Modeling, and Incident Response
levels.description: Establish organizational security and privacy standards for web engineering. Conduct threat modeling on new features, embed automated static analysis into CI, manage vulnerability disclosures, and direct incident response.
examples: Conduct a lightweight threat model (e.g., using STRIDE) during feature design to catch security and privacy flaws before code is written.
Integrate automated client-side security scanners (SAST, DAST, dependency vulnerability scanning) into the continuous integration pipeline.
Establish a security review process for approving new third-party marketing tags, analytics scripts, and SDKs.
Author clear incident response runbooks for compromised npm dependencies, leaked client API keys, or active XSS exploits.
Define a secure-by-default component design system (e.g., automatic sanitization in text rendering components, strict link target handling with rel="noopener noreferrer").
Review and test web authentication handoffs (OAuth 2.0 PKCE, WebAuthn/Passkeys, magic links) for token interception and session replay risks.
Mentor engineering and product teams on the balance between business telemetry needs and legal privacy compliance (GDPR, CCPA).
Exit criterion: Lead a comprehensive frontend threat-modeling session for an auth or payment flow, document residual risks, and establish automated security regression checks in CI.

tracks.name: Web Performance
tracks.description: Deliver fast, smooth, and resilient web experiences driven by measurable metrics and user-centric outcomes. Master Core Web Vitals—Largest Contentful Paint (LCP ≤ 2.5s), Interaction to Next Paint (INP ≤ 200ms), and Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS ≤ 0.1)—evaluated at the 75th percentile of real-world visits. Distinguish between synthetic lab diagnostics (Lighthouse, WebPageTest) and field Real User Monitoring (RUM, CrUX). Optimize the critical rendering path, eliminate main-thread bottlenecks and long animation frames (LoAF), minimize layout instability, establish performance budgets, and enforce continuous regression monitoring in CI/CD.
tracks.resources:
MUST — web.dev: Web Vitals & Core Web Vitals Guide. L1–L3. The definitive baseline for user-centric performance metrics: LCP, INP, and CLS thresholds, calculation mechanisms, and target percentiles (p75). Read through and inspect your site's metrics. 3–4 hours. https://web.dev/articles/vitals

MUST — web.dev: Understanding Lab vs. Field (RUM) Data. L2–L4. Crucial mental model explaining why a 100/100 Lighthouse score in DevTools does not guarantee high real-world user performance, and how Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) works. 2–3 hours. https://web.dev/articles/lab-and-field-data-differences

MUST — Chrome for Developers: Long Animation Frames API (LoAF). L3–L5. Master the primary modern browser diagnostic tool for tracking and debugging slow interactions, long script execution, and frame render delays that harm INP. 2–4 hours. https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/long-animation-frames

MUST — Chrome DevTools: Analyze Runtime and Loading Performance. L2–L5. Deep-dive into reading CPU flame charts, user timing tracks, layout shift clusters, network waterfalls, and simulated 4G / CPU throttling profiles. 4–6 hours of hands-on tracing. https://developer.chrome.com/docs/devtools/performance

USEFUL — web.dev: Optimize Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) & Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS). L2–L4. Actionable breakdown of the four LCP sub-parts (TTFB, Resource Load Delay, Resource Load Duration, Element Render Delay) and layout stability techniques. 3–4 hours. https://web.dev/articles/optimize-lcp and https://web.dev/articles/optimize-cls

USEFUL — WebPageTest: Documentation and Testing Capabilities. L3–L5. Run repeatable synthetic multi-run lab audits across real mobile hardware, global locations, and custom network profiles. 2–3 hours. https://docs.webpagetest.org/

levels.name: Performance Foundations and Measurement Basics
levels.description: Understand what makes web pages fast or slow from a user perspective. Distinguish core loading, rendering, and interaction milestones, and use browser DevTools to capture baseline performance observations under realistic network and CPU constraints.
examples: Define the Core Web Vitals metrics and their good thresholds: LCP (≤ 2.5s), INP (≤ 200ms), and CLS (≤ 0.1) at the 75th percentile.
Explain the difference between lab data (synthetic, controlled, reproducible) and field data (RUM, diverse hardware, real network conditions).
Run a basic Lighthouse audit and interpret performance scores, opportunities, and diagnostics without treating the score as an absolute pass/fail.
Record a performance trace with 4x or 6x CPU throttling and simulated mobile 4G network to observe low-end device constraints.
Identify and eliminate obvious layout shifts by setting explicit width and height attributes or aspect-ratio on images, videos, and embedded iframes.
Optimize critical image delivery using modern formats (WebP, AVIF), responsive srcset, and appropriate decoding="async".
Explain why putting render-blocking synchronous scripts in the HTML <head> degrades first-paint milestones.
Exit criterion: Audit a sluggish page, identify its LCP element and main layout shift culprits, and fix image sizing and script loading order.

levels.name: LCP and the Critical Loading Path
levels.description: Diagnose and optimize Largest Contentful Paint (LCP). Deconstruct LCP into its four distinct sub-phases, eliminate render-blocking dependencies, and optimize asset delivery.
examples: Deconstruct LCP into its four sub-parts: Time to First Byte (TTFB), Resource Load Delay, Resource Load Duration, and Element Render Delay.
Ensure the LCP image or text element is discoverable directly in the initial HTML response rather than dynamically fetched after client-side JavaScript executes.
Use `<link rel="preload" as="image" fetchpriority="high">` selectively on the genuine LCP resource and explain the danger of preloading too many assets.
Eliminate render-blocking CSS and fonts by inlining critical styles, deferring non-critical sheets, and using font-display: swap.
Implement modern resource compression (Brotli/Gzip) and CDN caching strategies to minimize network transfer times.
Debug Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) clusters caused by dynamically injected web fonts (FOUT/FOIT) using size-adjust and fallback font metric overrides.
Verify that lazy-loading (loading="lazy") is never placed on above-the-fold LCP images.
Exit criterion: Reduce LCP below 2.5s on a test page by resolving resource load delays and optimizing the critical rendering path.

levels.name: INP, Main-Thread Work, and Interaction Responsiveness
levels.description: Diagnose and fix interaction responsiveness bottlenecks to satisfy Interaction to Next Paint (INP). Break up long tasks, minimize input delay, avoid layout thrashing, and optimize event handler execution.
examples: Explain how INP measures the full interaction lifecycle: Input Delay (waiting for main thread), Processing Duration (running callbacks), and Presentation Delay (rendering the next frame).
Locate long tasks (> 50ms) in Chrome DevTools Performance traces and identify which specific function call monopolizes the main thread.
Yield the main thread during heavy computation using modern scheduler primitives (scheduler.yield(), requestAnimationFrame, or setTimeout fallback).
Use the Long Animation Frames (LoAF) API to capture slow frames and identify culprit scripts impacting interaction latency in the field.
Identify and eliminate forced synchronous layouts (layout thrashing) caused by interleaved DOM measurements and style mutations inside loops.
Debounce or throttle expensive visual event listeners (scroll, resize, mousemove) or replace them with native browser observers.
Provide immediate visual feedback (optimistic UI or loading states) for user taps before launching heavy asynchronous operations.
Exit criterion: Profile a laggy interaction, locate the main-thread bottleneck using a flame chart, break up the work, and bring INP under 200ms.

levels.name: Real User Monitoring (RUM) and Field Telemetry
levels.description: Implement and analyze Real User Monitoring (RUM) pipelines to observe real-world Core Web Vitals across geographic regions, device tiers, and user journeys. Connect lab audits to production business metrics.
examples: Integrate the web-vitals JavaScript library into client telemetry to capture LCP, INP, CLS, and LoAF attributions from real user sessions.
Analyze field data using the 75th percentile (p75) distribution rather than misleading arithmetic averages or medians.
Query and interpret the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) via BigQuery, CrUX API, or PageSpeed Insights to establish historical baselines.
Correlate real user Core Web Vitals improvements with core business indicators (conversion rate, bounce rate, session duration).
Segment RUM data by device class (low-end mobile vs. desktop), connection type (4G vs. WiFi), geography, and operating system.
Diagnose performance regressions caused by third-party scripts (tag managers, chat widgets, analytics) and isolate them using off-main-thread workers (e.g., Partytown) or deferred loading.
Build custom performance dashboards highlighting LCP element candidates, worst interaction selectors, and layout shift sources.
Exit criterion: Set up a working web-vitals RUM telemetry collector, generate a p75 dashboard, and pinpoint one production regression affecting low-end mobile users.

levels.name: Performance Systems, Budgets, and Culture
levels.description: Establish an organizational engineering standard for performance. Enforce performance budgets in CI/CD, govern bundle sizes, design architectural performance patterns (SSR/SSG/islands), and mentor teams to prevent performance decay.
examples: Define and enforce automated performance budgets in continuous integration (bundle size limits, lighthouse CI score floors, image size caps).
Evaluate architectural rendering trade-offs: Client-Side Rendering (CSR), Server-Side Rendering (SSR), Static Site Generation (SSG), Streaming SSR, and selective hydration.
Conduct bundle analysis to detect duplicate dependencies, un-tree-shaken imports, and heavy libraries, replacing them with lightweight alternatives.
Establish a company-wide "Performance Definition of Done" for all newly released features and design components.
Conduct architectural performance reviews for major product features before technical implementation begins.
Design resilient fallbacks for degraded networks (offline caching, skeleton screens, degraded asset resolution).
Mentor engineering and product teams on maintaining performance hygiene, treating performance as an ongoing feature rather than a one-off cleanup task.
Exit criterion: Implement an automated PR bundle-size and performance gate in CI, and publish an architectural performance playbook adopted by the engineering team.

tracks.name: Go & Gin
tracks.description: Building and maintaining real services in Go, using the standard library and Gin. Progress grows from a small working feature to concurrent, diagnosable services with clear ownership of resources and dependencies. Each level builds on previous project work; reading documentation or completing a tutorial alone does not establish a level. HTTP contracts, database design, security policy, and deployment are developed in their dedicated tracks; this track focuses on implementing them idiomatically in Go.
tracks.resources:
Core:
Go documentation: https://go.dev/doc/
Gin documentation: https://gin-gonic.com/en/docs/
Practice: keep examples, tests, profiling notes, and decisions from a maintained service. Revisit earlier decisions as its requirements grow.

levels.name: First Maintained Go Feature
levels.description: Implements a small useful feature in an actual project, with review or guidance where needed. Uses packages, structs, functions, slices, maps, and explicit error handling to keep behavior understandable. Can build, run, change, and test the feature locally and explain the path from input to output.
examples: Add a Gin endpoint used by the project UI and return a typed JSON response with appropriate status codes.
Validate request fields and handle an expected failure without panicking or exposing internal errors.
Add table-driven tests for the feature logic and an httptest request covering the endpoint.
Manage the module with go.mod, format code with gofmt, and document the local run command.

levels.name: Complete Service Feature
levels.description: Independently delivers a feature that crosses HTTP handling, application logic, and persistence or an external dependency. Applies Go interfaces at real boundaries, uses context cancellation and timeouts, and owns cleanup of resources. Uses Gin routing, middleware, and binding without hiding business rules inside framework-specific handlers.
examples: Implement a project workflow with several endpoints and a database repository, including not-found and conflict cases.
Pass request context into database or HTTP calls and close response bodies and other owned resources.
Add reusable request logging and error translation middleware without duplicating business decisions.
Run integration tests against a real disposable database and test handlers with httptest.

levels.name: Concurrent and Operable Service
levels.description: Maintains a Go service through normal changes and production failures. Introduces bounded concurrency for a concrete workload, handles cancellation and shutdown, and checks races and resource leaks. Connects useful service diagnostics to the shared observability setup and demonstrates that the service behaves predictably under load.
examples: Build a bounded worker pool for an actual background workload with cancellation and explicit error propagation.
Run go test -race on relevant workloads and fix a demonstrated data race or unsafe shared-state design.
Implement graceful HTTP shutdown and stop workers without losing acknowledged work.
Use pprof and project load tests to investigate memory retention, excessive allocation, or goroutine growth.

levels.name: Complex Service Evolution
levels.description: Changes a service with interacting dependencies and significant concurrency while preserving its external behavior. Uses measurements to improve throughput or latency, keeps failure handling bounded, and simplifies package boundaries when change reveals coupling. Demonstrates improvements with repeatable tests and operational evidence.
examples: Use benchmarks and profiles to improve a measured bottleneck, recording the baseline and the resulting trade-offs.
Test cancellation, slow dependencies, partial failures, and shutdown while requests are in flight.
Refactor an overloaded package or Gin handler into cohesive responsibilities while retaining contract coverage.
Add fuzz tests to an input parser or transformation used by the project and fix the failures they reveal.

levels.name: Sustained Go Service Ownership
levels.description: Owns the long-term behavior of a Go service or related services across substantial changes in requirements and load. Combines language, runtime, concurrency, and tooling knowledge to resolve difficult incidents and evolve the code safely. Produces reusable guidance grounded in the project and can help another contributor maintain it.
examples: Deliver a significant runtime, dependency, or service-internal migration with compatibility tests and an exercised recovery plan.
Resolve an incident involving several factors such as contention, allocation pressure, cancellation, and dependency latency.
Establish project-specific performance and concurrency checks based on observed regressions.
Document a maintained example and review checklist, then verify that another contributor can change and troubleshoot the service.

tracks.name: Node.js & NestJS
tracks.description: Developing and operating server applications with Node.js, TypeScript, and NestJS. Covers server runtime behavior, modules and dependency injection, asynchronous work, streams, testing, and service evolution. Builds on JavaScript and TypeScript knowledge in Web Platform while focusing on server processes and resources. Every level is demonstrated by useful changes in a real project.
tracks.resources:
Core:
Node.js learning documentation: https://nodejs.org/learn
NestJS documentation: https://docs.nestjs.com/
NestJS testing: https://docs.nestjs.com/fundamentals/testing
Practice: preserve request tests, failure cases, runtime measurements, and upgrade notes from the service.

levels.name: First NestJS Feature
levels.description: Adds a small working feature to an actual NestJS application. Uses a controller for HTTP interaction and a provider for application behavior, and registers dependencies in a module. Understands promises and async/await sufficiently to return the real operation result and expose failures predictably.
examples: Implement an endpoint consumed by the project, using a controller, injectable provider, and explicit request and response shapes.
Validate incoming data at runtime rather than relying only on TypeScript types.
Test the provider and send a real HTTP request in an end-to-end test.
Handle rejected promises and document how to configure and start the local server.

levels.name: Integrated Application Module
levels.description: Independently delivers a project workflow with persistence and an external integration. Organizes NestJS modules around actual responsibilities, keeps dependency boundaries explicit, and uses framework mechanisms for cross-cutting behavior. Makes database and network failures visible to callers without leaking implementation details.
examples: Build a cohesive module with deliberate imports and exports, keeping its internal providers private where possible.
Use pipes, guards, interceptors, or exception filters for a demonstrated validation, access-control, or request-processing need.
Test the workflow against a real disposable database and stub a controlled external boundary.
Set dependency timeouts, validate configuration on startup, and avoid circular provider dependencies.

levels.name: Predictable Runtime and Background Work
levels.description: Maintains a Node.js service with concurrent requests, streaming data, or background work. Distinguishes asynchronous I/O from CPU-bound execution and limits the amount of work held in memory. Handles process signals, worker lifecycle, and request diagnostics as part of operating the actual service.
examples: Stream a project import or export with backpressure instead of buffering the full payload in memory.
Move a measured CPU-heavy task to worker threads or a separate worker process and bound its concurrency.
Implement graceful shutdown that stops accepting work and drains or safely releases in-flight tasks.
Measure event-loop delay, request duration, and memory growth during a representative load test.

levels.name: Runtime Diagnosis and Modular Evolution
levels.description: Resolves difficult behavior involving the event loop, dependency injection, memory, and external dependencies. Uses profiling and repeatable workloads to identify causes before changing architecture. Evolves NestJS modules and dependencies without breaking supported consumers or creating excessive framework coupling.
examples: Diagnose an actual memory leak using heap evidence and verify stable memory over a sustained workload.
Find a blocking operation or unbounded async fan-out and demonstrate improved tail latency after the change.
Investigate provider lifecycle and scope when request-scoped dependencies cause unexpected overhead or behavior.
Upgrade a major dependency or reorganize modules with integration and contract coverage for existing behavior.

levels.name: Sustained Node.js Service Ownership
levels.description: Owns Node.js and NestJS service behavior through substantial workload and product changes. Balances runtime constraints, module design, and operational cost using evidence from the project. Keeps upgrades, incident response, and performance work repeatable and makes the service maintainable by other contributors.
examples: Complete a Node.js or NestJS major-version migration with an exercised rollout and recovery procedure.
Resolve a complex incident involving resource exhaustion, asynchronous lifecycle, and slow downstream services.
Establish project-specific limits and regression checks for payload size, concurrency, event-loop delay, and memory.
Create and validate a service maintenance guide covering module boundaries, diagnostics, testing, and dependency upgrades.

tracks.name: Server APIs & Integrations
tracks.description: Implementing dependable contracts between the project, its clients, and external services. Focuses on request and response semantics, integration failure handling, compatibility, and realistic contract tests. Architectural selection of communication styles remains in System Design & Architecture; this track demonstrates the resulting behavior in working APIs.
tracks.resources:
Core:
HTTP semantics: https://httpwg.org/specs/rfc9110.html
OpenAPI specification: https://spec.openapis.org/oas/latest.html
Practice: maintain a contract, executable examples, and failure tests alongside each public integration.

levels.name: Useful HTTP Contract
levels.description: Delivers a small API used by a real client. Chooses meaningful HTTP methods and status codes, validates inputs, and returns predictable success and error shapes. Documents enough of the contract for a client developer to use it without reading the handler implementation.
examples: Implement and integrate a create-and-read workflow with explicit required fields and not-found behavior.
Define request and response examples in OpenAPI and verify that the running API matches them.
Cover invalid input and expected errors in HTTP-level tests.
Reject malformed or oversized requests and keep internal diagnostics out of client error messages.

levels.name: Complete External Integration
levels.description: Builds an API workflow involving several operations and an external service. Handles pagination, filtering, timeouts, and external error translation. Applies retries only when the operation can safely be repeated and makes integration behavior testable without depending on an uncontrolled live environment.
examples: Implement deterministic pagination and validate filter and sorting parameters for a project list endpoint.
Wrap an external API with a timeout budget and mapped errors that the project can act on.
Use a controlled stub or provider sandbox to test timeout, rejection, and malformed-response cases.
Add bounded retries with backoff for a repeatable operation and verify that non-repeatable calls are not blindly retried.

levels.name: Reliable Stateful Workflows
levels.description: Maintains APIs where repeated, delayed, or concurrent requests can alter business state. Makes idempotency, concurrency control, and webhook handling explicit. Tests end-to-end failure scenarios and provides correlation information that connects a client-visible failure to the underlying work.
examples: Implement idempotency keys for an operation that must tolerate client retries, including payload mismatch and concurrent duplicate requests.
Verify webhook signatures, reject replayed or stale events as appropriate, and process duplicate delivery safely.
Prevent lost updates using a version check or another explicit concurrency mechanism.
Test the client-visible outcome when a dependency completes work but its response is lost.

levels.name: Contract Evolution and Multiple Consumers
levels.description: Evolves an API used by multiple clients or versions without causing avoidable breakage. Measures actual consumer behavior, defines compatibility expectations, and plans deprecation with consumers. Diagnoses protocol and integration failures across system boundaries.
examples: Ship a compatible contract extension and verify old and new clients against it.
Migrate a breaking contract through a documented version or transition period with consumer checks.
Implement cache validation, conditional requests, or streaming where a measured project need justifies it.
Use contract tests and captured non-sensitive request metadata to resolve a cross-service integration regression.

levels.name: Sustained Integration Ownership
levels.description: Owns a set of important API contracts through dependency changes, incidents, and evolving product workflows. Uses evidence to balance consistency, latency, compatibility, and support cost. Makes integration maintenance repeatable through executable contracts, diagnostics, and clear ownership.
examples: Replace or substantially upgrade an external provider while preserving supported project workflows.
Exercise a provider outage and recovery scenario, including delayed callbacks and partially completed operations.
Establish contract compatibility checks and a deprecation process that actual consumers can follow.
Document integration limits and failure behavior and use incident findings to improve both contracts and tests.

tracks.name: Databases & Storage
tracks.description: Designing, querying, and evolving the data used by a real product. PostgreSQL is the primary relational database; Redis provides concrete practice with caching and temporary state. Progress includes correctness, concurrency, performance, migrations, and data lifecycle decisions. Backup scheduling and recovery exercises are covered in Reliability & Incident Response; this track supplies the database-specific knowledge needed for them.
tracks.resources:
Core:
PostgreSQL documentation and tutorial: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tutorial.html
Redis development documentation: https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/
Practice: keep schema migrations, representative query plans, integration tests, and data consistency checks with the project.

levels.name: Persistent Project Feature
levels.description: Stores and retrieves real project data in PostgreSQL. Models a small domain with explicit keys, required fields, relationships, and constraints. Writes parameterized queries and verifies persistence behavior through the application rather than relying only on mocked repositories.
examples: Create tables for a useful project feature with primary keys, foreign keys, and relevant uniqueness constraints.
Implement parameterized create, read, update, and delete operations and test missing and duplicate records.
Add a versioned schema migration and run it on a clean development database.
Use joins and basic aggregation to answer an actual project query without loading every record into application memory.

levels.name: Consistent Workflows and Querying
levels.description: Implements multi-step data changes with transaction boundaries matching the business invariant. Uses indexes and query plans for actual access patterns, and maintains representative integration data. Understands connection pooling and avoids holding database resources across unrelated slow operations.
examples: Wrap a multi-table update in a transaction and test that a failed step leaves the required invariant intact.
Choose an index for a real query, inspect EXPLAIN output, and measure the change on representative data.
Remove an N+1 query pattern in an endpoint and verify result correctness and query count.
Configure a bounded connection pool and ensure transactions release connections on error and cancellation.

levels.name: Concurrency, Caching, and Safe Changes
levels.description: Maintains correctness when requests overlap and schema changes reach a running application. Uses Redis for a justified cache or temporary-state use case and defines expiration and invalidation behavior. Tests concurrent updates, stale data, and cache failure instead of assuming sequential execution.
examples: Prevent overselling, duplicate allocation, or another project-specific race using constraints, locking, or optimistic concurrency.
Deliver an additive schema migration and backfill that remain compatible with old and new application versions.
Implement cache-aside behavior with bounded TTLs and verify that a Redis outage does not silently corrupt authoritative data.
Test cache invalidation and concurrent refresh behavior for a frequently read project resource.

levels.name: Measured Data Performance and Evolution
