levels.description: Diagnoses query, lock, and storage bottlenecks using evidence from realistic workloads. Evolves larger datasets without prolonged blocking or uncontrolled load. Weighs relational storage, object storage, and specialized stores according to actual access and consistency requirements.
examples: Investigate a slow query with EXPLAIN ANALYZE in a safe environment and compare plans and latency after the fix.
Diagnose lock contention or a deadlock and adjust transaction order, scope, or access patterns.
Run a resumable, observable data backfill with bounded batches and a verified restart procedure.
Address cache stampedes or hot keys and measure the impact on both Redis and the source database.

levels.name: Sustained Data Ownership
levels.description: Owns data correctness and evolution through significant product and workload changes. Evaluates capacity, availability, retention, and migration options from project evidence and verifies the consequences of each choice. Can reconcile data after failures and explain the consistency guarantees available to the product.
examples: Execute a substantial schema or database migration with reconciliation checks, staged cutover, and a tested recovery procedure.
Use measured workload and operational constraints to justify a scaling decision and validate its impact.
Test replica-lag or failover behavior where replicas are used and document which reads require current data.
Implement a product data lifecycle covering retention, deletion, related records, cached copies, and audit evidence.

tracks.name: Messaging & Background Jobs
tracks.description: Implementing and operating asynchronous work with RabbitMQ and application workers. Covers delivery guarantees, acknowledgements, idempotency, retries, dead-letter handling, concurrency, and message evolution. Levels are based on a useful project workload such as notifications, imports, or media processing. System Design covers when asynchronous communication is appropriate; this track proves that the chosen workflow survives real failures.
tracks.resources:
Core:
RabbitMQ tutorials and documentation: https://www.rabbitmq.com/tutorials
Practice: document the lifecycle of one business operation, then exercise worker crashes, duplicate delivery, unavailable dependencies, and replay.

levels.name: Useful Background Job
levels.description: Moves an appropriate project task into a worker and connects it to the application through RabbitMQ. Makes the message payload and completion behavior explicit. Uses acknowledgements deliberately and verifies that an ordinary job can be traced from submission to its useful result.
examples: Process a real notification, import, or report request outside the interactive HTTP path.
Declare the queue and routing needed for the workflow and validate the incoming message shape.
Acknowledge work after its required side effect completes and expose a basic job outcome.
Run an integration test with a real broker and a worker, including a rejected message.

levels.name: Safe Retry and Duplicate Handling
levels.description: Makes a worker safe to retry and restart. Distinguishes transient and permanent failures, bounds retries, and records enough information to diagnose failed work. Treats repeated delivery as an expected possibility and validates idempotency at the business-operation boundary.
examples: Use a stable operation identifier and a database constraint or deduplication record to prevent a duplicated side effect.
Crash the worker after the side effect but before acknowledgement and verify that redelivery remains safe.
Apply bounded delayed retries for transient failures and route poison messages to a dead-letter destination.
Configure message durability and publisher confirms appropriately and test a failed publish.

levels.name: Consistent and Observable Workflow
levels.description: Coordinates asynchronous work with database changes and makes backlog behavior visible. Uses an outbox or another explicit consistency strategy where a database update must lead to a message. Controls consumer concurrency and prefetch according to dependency capacity and latency requirements.
examples: Implement a transactional outbox for a real state change and verify recovery after publishing is interrupted.
Expose queue depth, oldest-message age, processing time, retry volume, and dead-letter volume.
Set bounded concurrency and prefetch, then test that a slow dependency does not exhaust the worker.
Provide a controlled replay procedure that retains idempotency and records which failed jobs were retried.

levels.name: Complex Message Flow and Evolution
levels.description: Maintains several interacting asynchronous steps and handles ordering, compatibility, and partial completion explicitly. Evolves message contracts while existing messages and consumers remain active. Tests failure and recovery paths at workflow level rather than verifying only individual handlers.
examples: Deploy a compatible message schema change and test older queued messages against the new consumer.
Handle late or out-of-order events with explicit sequence or state checks where order matters.
Implement and test a compensating action for a partially completed multi-step workflow.
Load-test a burst of jobs and tune routing, concurrency, and backpressure using measured completion latency.

levels.name: Sustained Asynchronous System Ownership
levels.description: Owns asynchronous workflows through broker disruptions, large backlogs, and major application changes. Makes recovery capacity and business completion guarantees explicit. Uses incident evidence and controlled exercises to improve the system while avoiding unsupported claims of end-to-end exactly-once delivery.
examples: Exercise broker interruption and worker replacement, then reconcile submitted operations with their final business outcomes.
Recover a significant backlog without overwhelming downstream services or starving new critical work.
Migrate a queue topology or worker generation with compatible payloads and a tested rollback or recovery path.
Maintain a runbook that explains duplicate handling, message retention, replay permissions, and the limits of delivery guarantees.

tracks.name: Backend Application Security
tracks.description: Protecting server-side identities, permissions, data, and integrations throughout a real project. Builds on browser security knowledge but owns server enforcement, tenant boundaries, secrets handling, dependency risk, and verification. Uses established identity and cryptographic libraries and services. Progress is demonstrated through implemented controls and repeatable abuse-case tests, not security terminology alone.
tracks.resources:
Core:
OWASP Application Security Verification Standard: https://owasp.org/projects/asvs
Practice: select relevant verification requirements for the project, connect them to controls and tests, and revisit them after significant changes.

levels.name: Secure Feature Boundary
levels.description: Implements basic server-side protections for an actual feature. Treats every external input as untrusted, keeps secrets out of source control and responses, and checks access on the server. Verifies common invalid and unauthorized requests in the same workflow used by real clients.
examples: Validate request data and use parameterized database queries in the project feature.
Protect a private endpoint with an established authentication mechanism and test unauthenticated access.
Read secrets from the configured secret source and remove sensitive data from logs and error responses.
Bound request body size and validate uploaded file metadata and permitted processing behavior where uploads exist.

levels.name: Identity and Authorization Workflows
levels.description: Delivers complete identity and permission behavior using supported libraries or an identity provider. Separates authentication from authorization and checks object-level access for every relevant operation. Tests credential and session failure cases and handles account recovery without bypassing the normal trust boundary.
examples: Implement login and logout with secure session or token validation, expiration, and revocation behavior appropriate to the project.
When the project stores passwords, use a supported password-hashing library and a reviewed recovery flow.
Test that one user cannot read, edit, or delete another user’s private object by changing an identifier.
Apply rate limits and useful audit events to sensitive operations without logging credentials or tokens.

levels.name: Threat-Informed Service Protection
levels.description: Models realistic abuse paths across the service, its integrations, and deployment boundaries. Adds controls for the threats relevant to the product and verifies tenant and privilege boundaries. Integrates dependency and secret checks into normal delivery and investigates findings rather than treating a passing scanner as proof of safety.
examples: Create a threat model for an actual feature that records assets, trust boundaries, abuse cases, and planned controls.
Test tenant isolation across API queries, background jobs, caches, and file access where the project is multi-tenant.
Constrain user-influenced outbound requests to prevent SSRF and test blocked destinations and redirects.
Rotate a service credential and verify continued operation, least-privilege access, and removal of the old credential.

levels.name: Complex Authorization and Security Change
levels.description: Evolves security-sensitive behavior across multiple components and detects gaps that emerge from their interaction. Designs verification around business abuse cases and maintains a clear permission model as features grow. Coordinates remediation without creating new access paths or breaking legitimate workflows.
examples: Migrate roles or policies with tests covering default denial, privilege escalation, and existing user access.
Review a new integration for token scope, callback validation, secret storage, and revocation.
Investigate and fix a relevant dependency vulnerability, validating exposure and behavior after the update.
Run authorized negative tests in a controlled environment against realistic attack paths and record remediation evidence.

levels.name: Sustained Security Ownership
levels.description: Maintains the project’s security posture through substantial product changes and incidents. Prioritizes controls according to actual impact and exposure, keeps verification requirements current, and exercises response and recovery. Makes security work repeatable for contributors without requiring bespoke cryptography or a dedicated security organization.
examples: Review the project against a justified subset of OWASP ASVS and track each requirement to evidence or an explicit remediation decision.
Exercise a compromised credential or account scenario, including containment, revocation, investigation, and recovery.
Complete a security-sensitive architectural change with abuse-case tests and an independently reviewable permission model.
Establish a practical vulnerability intake, dependency maintenance, and access-review routine and improve it using actual findings.

tracks.name: Infrastructure & Environments
tracks.description: Provisioning and maintaining the environments that run a real product. Starts with Linux, networking, Docker, and a working server or managed service; grows into Terraform-managed infrastructure and practical Kubernetes operation at higher levels. Covers environment configuration, access, resource capacity, and reproducibility. Pipeline automation belongs to CI/CD & Releases; recovery objectives and incident management belong to Reliability & Incident Response.
tracks.resources:
Core:
Ubuntu Server documentation: https://ubuntu.com/server/docs/
Docker: https://docs.docker.com/get-started/
Higher levels:
Terraform tutorials: https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/tutorials
Kubernetes basics: https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/kubernetes-basics/
Practice: maintain the configuration needed to recreate the actual project environment, with secrets stored separately.

levels.name: Working Project Environment
levels.description: Runs a useful project service on a Linux server or managed environment and can perform basic maintenance with guidance. Understands the concrete route from DNS to the listening application. Configures a small environment deliberately and records enough information to repeat its setup.
examples: Deploy the project service, inspect its process and logs, and verify the expected listening address and port.
Configure DNS and HTTPS for an actual project endpoint and check certificate validity.
Use SSH keys and a restricted service account, and expose only the required network ports.
Document environment variables, persistent data locations, and the commands needed to restart the service.

levels.name: Repeatable Containerized Environments
levels.description: Independently runs the application and its dependencies using containers and clear environment configuration. Understands process, network, filesystem, and resource boundaries sufficiently to diagnose common failures. Separates durable data from replaceable containers and can recreate a project environment reliably.
examples: Build an application image with a small runtime footprint, a non-root user where supported, and no embedded credentials.
Use Docker Compose to run the service, PostgreSQL, and the dependencies actually needed by the project.
Configure persistent volumes, health checks, network connectivity, and restart behavior and verify container replacement.
Diagnose a failed deployment caused by DNS, file permissions, port binding, disk space, or configuration.

levels.name: Maintained Production Environment
levels.description: Operates distinct project environments with controlled access and predictable configuration. Applies routine system and container updates, manages resource limits, and monitors capacity. Verifies that another environment can be created from maintained configuration rather than relying on undocumented manual setup.
examples: Create separate staging and production environments with explicit secrets and data boundaries.
Apply a server or image update through staging, then verify production behavior and a recovery procedure.
Set CPU, memory, and storage expectations and investigate resource pressure using system and container tools.
Recreate a staging environment from maintained scripts or configuration and record the remaining manual dependencies.

levels.name: Terraform and Kubernetes in a Real Project
levels.description: Uses Terraform to provision an actual project environment and runs an application workload in Kubernetes. Reviews infrastructure changes before applying them, protects state, and understands the Kubernetes objects and probes required by the workload. Diagnoses ordinary scheduling, configuration, networking, and rollout failures.
examples: Manage project infrastructure with Terraform using protected remote state and backend-supported locking; review the plan before applying.
Deploy a workload with Deployment, Service, configuration, secret references, and an ingress or gateway appropriate to the cluster.
Configure resource requests and limits plus readiness, liveness, and startup probes according to actual application behavior.
Diagnose a failed rollout or pending/crashing pod using events, logs, resource state, and network checks.
Recreate the environment from Terraform and workload manifests, then verify application behavior and persistent-data dependencies.

levels.name: Sustained Infrastructure Evolution
levels.description: Maintains Terraform and Kubernetes environments through meaningful changes in load, topology, and platform versions. Handles drift, state changes, access boundaries, upgrades, and scaling using project evidence. Keeps infrastructure understandable and recoverable without assuming a large platform team or requiring self-managed control-plane expertise.
examples: Refactor or import Terraform-managed resources with an inspected plan and controlled state handling that avoids unintended replacement.
Perform a Kubernetes or node-pool upgrade and test workload availability, disruption settings, storage, and recovery.
Apply least-privilege RBAC and appropriate network restrictions and verify permitted and denied application paths.
Tune scaling and resource allocation from measured demand, reliability needs, and actual infrastructure cost.
Detect configuration drift and demonstrate that another contributor can reproduce and maintain the environment using the recorded procedure.

tracks.name: CI/CD & Releases
tracks.description: Automating the path from a reviewed change to a verified running release, with GitLab CI/CD as the practical platform. Covers pipeline jobs, runners, artifacts, images, environments, deployment controls, database changes, and recovery. Progress is based on pipelines used by the project and release outcomes. Higher levels integrate Terraform and Kubernetes while keeping infrastructure ownership in its dedicated track.
tracks.resources:
Core:
GitLab CI/CD documentation: https://docs.gitlab.com/ci/
Practice: retain pipeline configuration, release records, deployment checks, and evidence from an exercised recovery path.

levels.name: Useful Continuous Integration
levels.description: Adds a working GitLab pipeline to the actual repository and uses it to check changes. Understands jobs, stages, runners, and job failure well enough to diagnose a failed build. Keeps validation commands reproducible locally and in CI.
examples: Create .gitlab-ci.yml jobs that install dependencies reproducibly, run formatting or lint checks, and execute relevant tests.
Build the application and retain a useful artifact with an explicit expiration policy.
Inspect runner logs to fix a real pipeline failure without suppressing the failing check.
Run merge-request validation with rules that avoid unnecessary duplicate pipelines.

levels.name: Automated Deployment to an Environment
levels.description: Builds and deploys a traceable project release through GitLab. Separates dependency caches from release artifacts, scopes secrets to the work that needs them, and verifies the deployed result. Can identify which source revision and artifact are running in the environment.
examples: Build a versioned container image once, publish it, and deploy that exact artifact to staging.
Configure environment-scoped variables and protected credentials without exposing secrets to untrusted jobs or logs.
Add a post-deployment smoke test that verifies an actual project workflow.
Record the commit and artifact identity of the release and deploy a previous known-good artifact in staging.

levels.name: Controlled Production Releases
levels.description: Uses the pipeline for recurring production changes with explicit deployment and recovery behavior. Coordinates application releases with database compatibility, serializes conflicting deployments, and verifies results beyond job success. Exercises both application rollback and recovery when a data change cannot safely be reversed.
examples: Promote the tested artifact to production with appropriate environment protection and deployment permissions.
Use resource groups or another deliberate mechanism to prevent conflicting deployments to the same environment.
Deliver an expand-and-contract database change that tolerates old and new application versions during rollout.
Verify a real release using smoke tests and operational signals, then exercise rollback or forward recovery as appropriate.

levels.name: Infrastructure and Kubernetes Delivery
levels.description: Integrates infrastructure and Kubernetes changes into a reviewable release flow. Controls credentials and change boundaries, prevents concurrent infrastructure mutations, and checks rollout health. Optimizes pipeline structure only where measurements reveal meaningful feedback or reliability problems.
examples: Run Terraform validation and plan in CI and apply a reviewed plan with state protection and appropriate deployment authorization.
Deploy the application to Kubernetes and verify rollout status, readiness, and a representative client workflow.
Implement a gradual rollout for a justified change and test abort and recovery behavior when health deteriorates.
Use job dependencies, parallelism, or targeted caching to reduce measured feedback time without skipping necessary checks.
Restrict runners, tokens, and deployment jobs according to their trust level and verify that ordinary contributions cannot access production secrets.

levels.name: Sustained Delivery System Ownership
levels.description: Owns release automation across substantial application and infrastructure changes. Makes artifact provenance, delivery failure recovery, and pipeline maintenance practical for the project. Uses actual delivery outcomes to improve speed and reliability without turning pipeline conventions into unnecessary process.
examples: Exercise recovery from a failed deployment involving application, infrastructure, and a partially completed migration.
Preserve traceability from source revision through build and deployed artifact, adding provenance or signing checks where project needs justify them.
Measure delivery lead time, release failures, and recovery time and use the findings to remove a demonstrated bottleneck.
Upgrade or replace runner and pipeline components while keeping deployment access controlled and releases reproducible.
Document and validate a release playbook that another contributor can use to deploy and recover the project.

tracks.name: Observability
tracks.description: Making real project behavior explainable with metrics, logs, traces, dashboards, and actionable alerts. Uses OpenTelemetry, Prometheus, and Grafana as practical reference tools. Tracks system health and user-visible technical behavior; product adoption, funnels, and hypothesis validation belong to Product Analytics & Experiments. Reliability uses the signals created here to define and maintain service objectives.
tracks.resources:
Core:
OpenTelemetry concepts: https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/
Prometheus: https://prometheus.io/docs/introduction/overview/
Grafana: https://grafana.com/docs/grafana/latest/
Practice: start each dashboard or alert with the operational question and action it is meant to support.

levels.name: Visible Project Behavior
levels.description: Adds useful diagnostics to a running project feature and uses them to investigate a real or deliberately reproduced failure. Makes logs structured and searchable, exposes basic health information, and avoids recording sensitive payloads. Can connect an observed error to a particular operation.
examples: Add structured request and error logs with a correlation identifier and meaningful operation context.
Expose a health endpoint that distinguishes process availability from required readiness checks.
Collect request count, error count, and request duration for the service and inspect them during a reproduced failure.
Verify that credentials, tokens, and unnecessary personal data are absent from the new diagnostics.

levels.name: Useful Dashboards and Alerts
levels.description: Builds a focused view of project health and routes actionable failures to a person responsible for responding. Selects metric types and labels deliberately, defines useful thresholds and evaluation windows, and tests alert behavior. Uses diagnostics to answer actual operational questions rather than collecting data without a purpose.
examples: Build a Grafana dashboard for traffic, errors, latency, and resource saturation using Prometheus metrics.
Choose bounded metric labels and avoid user IDs, request IDs, or raw URLs as unbounded label values.
Configure an alert with an owner, a runbook link, and a concrete response, then trigger and resolve it in a controlled test.
Investigate a reported slowdown by correlating deployment time, request metrics, and application logs.

levels.name: End-to-End Diagnosis
levels.description: Instruments a workflow across service and asynchronous boundaries using OpenTelemetry where appropriate. Connects traces, logs, and metrics while managing sampling and collection overhead. Measures important user journeys and background work so failures outside the main HTTP handler are visible.
examples: Trace an actual request through the API, database, and an external dependency with useful spans and context propagation.
Propagate or link trace context through a background job without placing secrets in message metadata.
Monitor queue age, worker failures, and scheduled-job completion for project workflows that can fail silently.
Use a trace and associated logs to identify the slow dependency behind an observed tail-latency regression.

levels.name: Signal Quality and Operational Coverage
levels.description: Improves diagnostic coverage for complex failures and reduces the cost and noise of telemetry. Relates alerts to user-visible reliability objectives, distinguishes symptoms from contributing causes, and tests behavior when monitoring components fail. Uses real incident and usage evidence to remove misleading signals.
examples: Implement alerts based on a project service objective and verify their behavior against short and sustained failures.
Reduce false positives or duplicate notifications using incident evidence and preserve detection of meaningful failures.
Tune trace sampling, log retention, and metric cardinality while preserving the ability to investigate important workflows.
Verify ingestion failure or missing-data detection so a silent telemetry outage is not interpreted as a healthy service.

levels.name: Sustained Observability Ownership
levels.description: Maintains an effective diagnostic system as services, infrastructure, and product workflows evolve. Uses incidents to identify missing evidence and improves instrumentation before the next similar failure. Balances privacy, retention, cost, and diagnostic value with explicit project decisions.
examples: Diagnose a failure spanning application, queue, database, and Kubernetes using correlated evidence.
Run a controlled failure exercise and measure whether dashboards, alerts, and traces enable the expected diagnosis.
Review telemetry access and retention and remove unnecessary sensitive or high-cost data while keeping required evidence.
Establish a maintained instrumentation checklist and verify that a new project feature arrives with useful operational coverage.

tracks.name: Reliability & Incident Response
tracks.description: Keeping a real product useful through failures, maintenance, and changing demand. Covers service objectives, backups and verified restoration, incident response, resilience testing, and operational learning. Uses signals from Observability and environments maintained in Infrastructure. Progress means demonstrably better recovery and fewer repeated failures, with responsibility scaled to the actual project.
tracks.resources:
Core:
Google SRE books and workbook: https://sre.google/books/
Practice: keep restoration evidence, incident timelines, recovery procedures, and follow-up outcomes from the project.

levels.name: Basic Recovery for a Running Project
levels.description: Maintains a running project with a known way to detect and recover from ordinary failures. Identifies the data and configuration that must survive a restart. Performs a real restoration exercise in an isolated environment and records what is needed to bring the service back.
examples: Document how to check service health, restart it safely, and confirm that a useful user workflow works afterward.
Create a backup of project data and restore it into a separate environment, checking data and application behavior.
Keep backup access and secrets separate from public application access.
Record the contact or owner and the first diagnostic steps for an unavailable service.

levels.name: Repeatable Maintenance and Incident Handling
levels.description: Runs routine maintenance and handles common incidents through a repeatable procedure. Automates backups, checks their completion, and tests restoration on a schedule suited to the project. Communicates the impact and records a factual incident timeline and follow-up work.
examples: Automate backups with a retention policy and an alert for missing or failed backup jobs.
Measure the time and data loss involved in restoration and compare them with the project’s needs.
Resolve a realistic service outage using the runbook and verify recovery through the affected user journey.
Write an incident review that explains contributing conditions and assign concrete improvements without blaming an individual.

levels.name: Defined Reliability and Failure Behavior
levels.description: Defines reliability expectations around actual user journeys and uses them to prioritize operational work. Establishes realistic recovery time and recovery point objectives and tests dependency failure behavior. Makes the trade-off between reliability work and feature delivery explicit for the project.
examples: Define a service-level indicator and objective for an important user journey using available operational data.
Specify RTO and RPO for critical data and demonstrate a recovery exercise that measures both.
Test slow or unavailable dependencies and verify timeouts, bounded retries, and graceful degradation where appropriate.
Use incident frequency and service-objective performance to prioritize a concrete reliability improvement.

levels.name: Complex Recovery and Resilience
levels.description: Handles failures that cross multiple components or involve partial data loss and delayed work. Tests capacity and recovery under representative conditions and coordinates application, infrastructure, and data changes. Improves resilience based on measured failure behavior instead of adding redundancy without a demonstrated need.
examples: Exercise loss of an application node or workload instance and verify routing, in-flight work, and recovery.
Restore database state and reconcile queued work and external side effects after a controlled partial-failure scenario.
Use load and recovery tests to identify a capacity limit and verify an appropriate degradation or scaling response.
Resolve an incident involving multiple contributors or components with explicit roles, communication, and a verified recovery checkpoint.

levels.name: Sustained Reliability Ownership
levels.description: Maintains reliability through substantial changes in product use and system design. Runs useful recovery exercises, reviews objectives, and tracks whether incident follow-ups actually prevent recurrence. Keeps the project supportable with its available people, infrastructure budget, and operational capacity.
examples: Complete a disaster-recovery exercise from documented configuration and backups and close the gaps it reveals.
Use service-objective performance and incident trends to revise reliability priorities and delivery decisions.
Reduce recurring operational work through a measured automation or design improvement and verify that failures remain diagnosable.
Validate operational handover with another contributor, including restoration, incident communication, and recovery of critical workflows.

tracks.name: Development Methods & Process Improvement
tracks.description: Applying Agile principles, Lean thinking, Scrum, Kanban, and XP practices to the actual work of a project team. Progress is cumulative: each level adds practical breadth and more difficult process decisions, rather than treating methods as successive maturity stages. Evaluates methods through feedback, flow, quality, and useful outcomes. Individual planning mechanics are developed in Planning & Work Organization; this track improves the way the team works as a system.
tracks.resources:
Core:
Agile principles: https://agilemanifesto.org/principles.html
Scrum Guide: https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html
Kanban Guide: https://kanbanguides.org/the-kanban-guide/2025.5/
Lean thinking: https://www.lean.org/explore-lean/what-is-lean/
XP: Kent Beck and Cynthia Andres, Extreme Programming Explained, 2nd edition (paid book; publisher overview): https://www.informit.com/store/extreme-programming-explained-embrace-change-9780321278654
Practice: record the problem, chosen practice, expected effect, observed result, and next adjustment.

levels.name: Visible Work and Short Feedback
levels.description: Applies a small set of development practices to a real project with other contributors or stakeholders. Makes work visible, delivers a useful increment, and obtains feedback before treating the work as finished. Can connect an adopted practice to the problem it is intended to solve.
examples: Track actual work on a board with explicit start and finish criteria and update it as work progresses.
Break a useful change into a short feedback cycle and demonstrate the result to a real stakeholder.
Agree a small Definition of Done covering the checks needed for the project’s current work.
Hold a short retrospective after delivery and carry out one specific improvement.

levels.name: Applied Scrum and Flow Practices
levels.description: Participates effectively in an actual Scrum cadence and applies explicit Kanban flow practices to project work. Can explain their different purposes without presenting them as competing maturity levels. Uses observed work and feedback to adjust commitments and improve how the team finishes work.
examples: Contribute to a real Sprint Goal, planning, review, and retrospective, and verify a usable increment against the Definition of Done.
Make workflow policies explicit and use work-in-progress limits to expose overloaded stages or blocked items.
Measure work-item age and cycle time and use the data to change a concrete team habit.
When using selected Scrum practices without the complete framework, describe the process accurately and record the intentional differences.

levels.name: Engineering Feedback and Lean Improvement
levels.description: Adds engineering and flow practices that address observed quality or delivery problems. Applies XP practices in real collaboration and uses Lean thinking to identify waiting, unnecessary work, and slow feedback. Tests process changes as hypotheses rather than assuming that adopting a named method guarantees improvement.
examples: Use pairing or another collaborative development practice on a difficult change and review its effect on rework and shared understanding.
Apply test-first development, continuous integration, and small refactoring steps to an actual feature or defect.
Map the path from request to usable change and remove a measured delay, handoff, or recurring source of rework.
Run a bounded process experiment with a baseline, expected effect, review date, and recorded result.

levels.name: Process Design for Changing Conditions
levels.description: Adjusts the team’s working approach when support load, uncertainty, dependencies, or team composition change. Combines practices with a clear rationale, preserves feedback and quality, and measures their effects. Avoids using activity counts or individual velocity as a substitute for useful outcomes.
examples: Adapt planning and flow policies when unpredictable support work repeatedly interrupts planned development.
Address an external dependency or approval bottleneck using an explicit agreement and measurable follow-up.
Compare delivery predictability, quality, and stakeholder feedback before and after a process change.
Retire a ceremony or rule that has ceased to serve its intended purpose while retaining the feedback it was meant to provide.

levels.name: Sustained Team Process Improvement
levels.description: Maintains an effective development process through significant project and team changes. Helps the team diagnose its own bottlenecks and make evidence-based improvements. Keeps methods understandable, adaptable, and sustainable while demonstrating better delivery outcomes over multiple cycles.
examples: Lead several improvement cycles and show which changes improved flow or quality and which were revised or reversed.
Help new contributors understand the purpose of current workflow policies and participate in improving them.
Resolve a persistent trade-off between urgent work, planned delivery, and quality using explicit policies and observed outcomes.
Leave a concise working agreement and review routine that the team can maintain without depending on one process owner.

tracks.name: Planning & Work Organization
tracks.description: Turning actual product goals into a realistic and adaptable sequence of work. Covers decomposition, priorities, estimates, uncertainty, dependencies, capacity, and delivery follow-through. Planning is evaluated through decisions and usable results, not adherence to an original forecast at any cost. Product Understanding & Requirements establishes why work matters; this track organizes its execution.
tracks.resources:
Core:
GitLab Engineering Workflow (a company practice to evaluate, not a universal standard): https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/workflow/
Scrum Guide: https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html
Practice: keep the original assumptions, scope decisions, delivery observations, and resulting adjustments for real work.

levels.name: Finish a Defined Piece of Work
levels.description: Takes a small real project task from clarification to a verified result. Identifies its expected outcome, acceptance criteria, dependencies, and immediate steps. Makes blockers visible early and updates the plan when new information appears.
examples: Clarify an ambiguous request with its stakeholder and record testable acceptance criteria.
Break the task into a few concrete implementation and verification steps.
Identify a missing decision, access dependency, or external input before it blocks completion.
Demonstrate the finished result and record any remaining work or changed assumptions.

levels.name: Plan a Complete Feature
levels.description: Independently plans and delivers a feature involving several tasks and collaborators. Slices work into usable increments, distinguishes essential scope from optional work, and treats estimates as forecasts with assumptions. Coordinates dependencies and includes testing, deployment, and support preparation in the plan.
examples: Create a sequence of vertical slices that each deliver observable behavior to the project.
Estimate a range or identify uncertainty and validate a risky assumption before committing to the full implementation.
Agree interface or dependency expectations with another contributor and track the required delivery order.
Include data migration, rollout, documentation, and operational checks where the feature requires them.

levels.name: Balance Team Capacity and Priorities
levels.description: Organizes several competing work items for an actual team while accounting for support, maintenance, and uncertainty. Makes scope and sequencing trade-offs visible and revisits them with stakeholders. Uses delivery observations to improve forecasts rather than hiding deviations.
examples: Prioritize a backlog using expected value, urgency, risk, effort, and explicit dependencies.
Reserve realistic capacity for support and maintenance using recent project evidence.
Replan after a dependency slips or a significant defect appears, agreeing the impact on scope and timing.
Compare expected and actual delivery for several items and identify a recurring source of forecasting error.

levels.name: Coordinate Complex Delivery
levels.description: Plans an initiative involving multiple components, uncertain technical work, and external dependencies. Uses milestones as evidence of reduced risk or delivered capability, and keeps a credible path to completion as conditions change. Makes decisions explicit when delivery, scope, and quality goals conflict.
examples: Create a dependency map and sequence a cross-component change so integration risks are tested early.
Use a time-bounded investigation to resolve a key uncertainty and update the delivery forecast from its result.
Agree a reduced but useful release scope when new information makes the original scope unrealistic.
Coordinate rollout, communication, support readiness, and fallback responsibilities across the participating contributors.

levels.name: Sustained Delivery Planning
levels.description: Maintains credible priorities and forecasts across a changing product roadmap. Balances feature work, reliability, security, and structural improvements with the people and resources actually available. Builds a planning process that makes uncertainty visible and helps the team make timely decisions.
examples: Plan and deliver several related increments while adapting the roadmap to user feedback and operational evidence.
Use historical delivery data and risk reviews to improve forecast ranges and communicate confidence honestly.
Resolve a recurring resource or dependency conflict through explicit prioritization and ownership agreements.
Review completed and abandoned work to improve future slicing, estimation, and stop-or-continue decisions.

tracks.name: Team Building & Development
tracks.description: Building a team that can deliver and maintain the project together. Covers the capabilities the project needs, onboarding, hiring or contributor selection, delegation, feedback, mentoring, and sustainable ownership. Every level requires real collaboration; a solo simulation does not demonstrate team-building competence. Formal authority is not required for early levels, but later levels involve actual responsibility for team capability and continuity.
tracks.resources:
Core:
GitLab Engineering Management handbook (context-specific examples): https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/engineering/careers/management/
Practice: retain non-sensitive role expectations, onboarding improvements, delegated outcomes, and evidence that team capability has grown. Keep confidential personnel details outside the matrix.

levels.name: Support Another Contributor
levels.description: Helps a real contributor become productive in the project. Explains the purpose and basic working practices, provides a manageable first task, and answers questions respectfully. Gives specific feedback on work and notices where the project makes collaboration unnecessarily difficult.
examples: Help another contributor set up the project and complete a useful first change.
Explain who owns an area, how changes are reviewed, and how to get help when blocked.
Give concrete, respectful review feedback and check that the recipient understands the reasoning.
Improve an onboarding instruction after observing where the contributor struggled.

levels.name: Delegation and Individual Growth
levels.description: Delegates a meaningful area of work with clear expectations and appropriate support. Uses regular conversations and actionable feedback to help another person become more independent. Distinguishes a skill gap from unclear requirements, missing access, or an overloaded workflow.
examples: Delegate a real feature or maintenance responsibility with an outcome, decision boundaries, and agreed check-ins.
Hold recurring development conversations or 1:1s and follow through on agreed support.
Create a practical learning opportunity tied to project work and review the resulting improvement.
Give timely feedback on an observable behavior and agree a specific next step without making personal judgments.

levels.name: Build a Capable Project Team
levels.description: Identifies the capabilities and ownership coverage needed by the project and helps assemble or expand the team accordingly. Participates in actual hiring or contributor selection with explicit, job-relevant criteria. Creates an onboarding and ownership plan that reduces dependence on a single person.
examples: Map required project responsibilities to current team capability and identify a concrete gap.
Use a structured interview or work discussion with consistent criteria in a real hiring or contributor-selection process.
Onboard the selected person with useful initial work, support contacts, and explicit expectations.
Share a critical operational or technical responsibility between contributors and verify the handover in practice.

levels.name: Develop Ownership and Resolve Team Gaps
levels.description: Improves team capability when responsibilities, performance expectations, or workload change. Handles difficult feedback and ownership gaps fairly and directly. Delegates decisions as well as tasks, balances autonomy with support, and addresses causes of overload rather than normalizing unsustainable effort.
examples: Agree a concrete improvement plan when repeated work outcomes fall short of shared expectations and review progress.
Resolve an ownership gap or overlapping responsibility that is causing delays or incidents.
Help a contributor take independent responsibility for a project area and verify their ability to maintain it.
Adjust workload, support rotation, or team responsibilities after evidence of repeated overload or concentration of knowledge.

levels.name: Sustained Team Capability
levels.description: Builds a team that maintains delivery and support through growth, changing priorities, and contributor transitions. Evaluates hiring, onboarding, delegation, and development by their actual effect on capability and continuity. Creates clear expectations and enough shared ownership for the project to function without constant intervention from one person.
examples: Plan and execute a contributor transition without losing maintenance or incident-response coverage.
Use outcomes from actual onboarding and selection to improve role expectations and assessment criteria.
Demonstrate that several contributors can independently lead changes and maintain their areas with effective collaboration.
Review team capacity, development needs, and ownership risks over multiple delivery cycles and act on the findings.

tracks.name: Communication & Collaborative Decisions
tracks.description: Creating shared understanding and making useful decisions with contributors, users, and stakeholders. Covers written context, feedback, facilitation, disagreement, expectations, and difficult conversations. Progress grows from clear communication about one task to resolving complex cross-functional decisions and maintaining healthy collaboration. Evidence comes from real interactions and their outcomes.
tracks.resources:
Core:
GitLab Communication handbook (practices to adapt to the project): https://handbook.gitlab.com/handbook/communication/
Practice: keep concise decision records, agreed actions, and examples of misunderstandings resolved; exclude private personal conversations.

levels.name: Clear Task Communication
levels.description: Communicates about actual project work with enough context for another person to respond or act. Checks understanding, separates observations from assumptions, and makes requests specific. Keeps stakeholders informed about completion, blockers, and changed expectations.
examples: Write an issue or change description explaining the problem, expected behavior, and relevant constraints.
Ask a focused clarification question and restate the resulting agreement before implementing an ambiguous request.
Report a blocker with its impact, the investigation already done, and the decision or help needed.
Demonstrate a finished change in language appropriate to the stakeholder and check their understanding.

levels.name: Useful Feedback and Discussion
levels.description: Participates in reviews and decisions with constructive, specific reasoning. Communicates trade-offs without assuming shared technical knowledge and chooses an appropriate communication channel. Captures agreements so contributors do not need to reconstruct them from scattered conversations.
examples: Explain two implementation options through their user impact, cost, and operational consequences.
Give review feedback that distinguishes a correctness issue, a project convention, and a personal preference.
Move a stalled written discussion into a focused conversation and record the decision afterward.
Provide an asynchronous progress update with outcomes, risks, and the next decision needed.

levels.name: Facilitation and Expectation Alignment
levels.description: Facilitates a real discussion involving different perspectives and leads it to a clear outcome. Makes constraints and disagreement explicit, ensures relevant people are heard, and identifies who will decide and act. Renegotiates expectations early when project facts change.
examples: Facilitate a planning, design, or retrospective session with a stated objective and concrete follow-up actions.
Align a technical constraint with a stakeholder’s product goal and agree an achievable alternative.
Record a consequential decision with its rationale, owner, assumptions, and review trigger.
Resolve a misunderstanding between contributors by checking facts and intended outcomes with both sides.

levels.name: Difficult Decisions and Conflict
levels.description: Handles consequential disagreement without avoiding the decision or turning it into a personal contest. Separates needs and constraints from proposed solutions, surfaces uncertainty, and uses evidence or a bounded experiment to move forward. Communicates difficult changes honestly and respectfully.
examples: Resolve a real disagreement about scope, design, or ownership by agreeing evaluation criteria and a decision process.
Negotiate a delivery or support expectation that cannot be met under current constraints and record the accepted trade-off.
Communicate an incident or missed commitment with clear impact, known facts, uncertainty, and the next update.
Revisit a decision when new evidence undermines its assumptions and help the participants update their position.

levels.name: Sustained Cross-Functional Collaboration
levels.description: Maintains effective collaboration through complex initiatives and changing participants. Builds communication habits that support timely decisions and understandable ownership. Identifies recurring sources of disagreement or missing context and improves how the project coordinates work.
examples: Align contributors and stakeholders on a substantial project change and sustain that agreement through implementation and rollout.
Improve a recurring communication failure using evidence from missed expectations, rework, or slow decisions.
Help other contributors facilitate decisions and handle disagreement independently.
Validate that decision records and communication routines allow a new participant to understand the project’s current commitments and rationale.

tracks.name: Product Understanding & Requirements
tracks.description: Understanding why the actual product exists, who uses it, which problems it solves, and how its value and constraints shape engineering decisions. Turns requests into testable problem statements and useful increments, connects technical work to product outcomes, and revisits assumptions after delivery. Planning organizes execution; this track establishes purpose, evidence, and the meaning of success.
tracks.resources:
Core:
GOV.UK Service Manual, learning about users and their needs: https://www.gov.uk/service-manual/user-research/start-by-learning-user-needs
Practice: use actual user observations, support cases, stakeholder discussions, and product behavior; distinguish confirmed needs from assumptions and requested solutions.

levels.name: Understand a Real User Problem
levels.description: Explains the purpose of the project and connects an assigned feature to a real user need. Identifies who is affected, what they are trying to accomplish, and how they currently cope. Clarifies the expected outcome before implementing a requested solution.
examples: Describe the product’s intended users, core problem, and main user journey in concrete language.
Discuss an actual request with a user or stakeholder and record the underlying problem separately from the proposed feature.
Observe or reproduce the current difficulty using the actual product and note relevant constraints.
Write acceptance criteria that show the user can complete the intended task, including an important failure case.

levels.name: Shape a Useful Product Change
levels.description: Investigates a problem using more than one source of project evidence and compares plausible solutions. Considers the existing user journey, business or service purpose, and implementation constraints. Proposes a small useful change with an explicit expected outcome and obtains feedback from affected people.
examples: Combine a user discussion with support feedback, product observations, or available usage evidence.
Compare a requested feature with a simpler workflow change and explain their value and cost.
Identify key business rules and edge cases with stakeholders before committing to a solution.
Review a prototype or small working increment with intended users and revise the requirements from their feedback.

levels.name: Own a Problem Through Delivery
levels.description: Follows a product problem from discovery through implementation and evaluation. Makes assumptions and success criteria explicit, prioritizes the riskiest unknowns, and coordinates product and engineering decisions. Checks whether the delivered change helped users and adjusts the next step from evidence.
examples: Create a concise problem brief with affected users, evidence, constraints, expected outcome, and unresolved assumptions.
Test a high-risk assumption through an interview, prototype, or limited release before expanding the implementation.
Deliver a useful increment with the analytics and feedback collection needed to evaluate the intended outcome.
Compare the result with the original problem and choose to extend, revise, or stop the proposed solution.

levels.name: Balance Product and Engineering Trade-Offs
levels.description: Handles product changes involving competing user needs, business constraints, and technical consequences. Connects engineering quality, reliability, and operational cost to the product’s purpose. Makes opportunity cost and uncertainty visible and helps stakeholders choose an appropriate scope and sequence.
examples: Evaluate a feature request against user impact, product direction, support burden, and ongoing infrastructure cost.
Identify when reliability, accessibility, or data correctness work directly addresses an important product problem.
Resolve conflicting requirements from different user groups with explicit criteria and a tested compromise.
Propose a staged solution that reduces a major uncertainty before committing to an expensive architecture or broad feature set.

levels.name: Sustained Product Engineering Ownership
levels.description: Helps guide the product through changing user needs and business conditions using evidence from delivered work. Maintains a clear link between the product’s purpose, engineering investment, and observed outcomes. Can challenge weak assumptions constructively and help the team avoid maintaining features that no longer serve a useful need.
examples: Use several delivery and feedback cycles to reshape a meaningful part of the product roadmap.
Recommend and carry out a supported decision to simplify, replace, or retire a feature whose value does not justify its cost.
Maintain shared understanding of key user journeys, business rules, product constraints, and unresolved risks as contributors change.
Demonstrate a substantial engineering decision whose measured product outcome supports the chosen trade-off.

tracks.name: Product Analytics & Experiments
tracks.description: Using evidence to determine whether a real product and its changes help the intended users. Covers meaningful events, task completion, funnels, activation, retention, segmentation, qualitative feedback, and hypothesis testing. Focuses on product outcomes rather than service health. Chooses evidence appropriate to the available traffic and avoids claiming causal effects from ordinary before-and-after observations.
tracks.resources:
Core:
Google HEART research, user-centered metrics: https://research.google/pubs/measuring-the-user-experience-on-a-large-scale-user-centered-metrics-for-web-applications/
Google Analytics event concepts (a concrete implementation reference, not a required vendor): https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9322688
Practice: define the decision first, then the metric, event semantics, quality checks, and interpretation limits. Collect only data needed for that purpose.

levels.name: Measure a Useful Product Action
levels.description: Instruments a real user action connected to the product’s purpose and checks that the data matches actual behavior. Defines what success and failure mean and uses a simple view of the evidence to answer a concrete question. Treats data collection and access as explicit project responsibilities.
examples: Choose a meaningful action such as completing onboarding, saving a result, or finishing a core workflow.
Define the event name, trigger, allowed properties, and identity behavior needed to measure that action.
Verify event delivery for success, failure, and repeated interaction without sending secrets or unnecessary personal data.
Inspect real usage or an explicitly identified validation session and report what is observed without overstating adoption.

levels.name: Understand a User Journey
levels.description: Measures a sequence of actions and investigates where users encounter difficulty. Distinguishes traffic, successful task completion, and returning use, and documents event and identity assumptions. Combines quantitative signals with user or support feedback to choose a practical improvement.
examples: Build a funnel for an actual user journey with explicit steps, time window, and population.
Check duplicate events, missing steps, internal traffic, and identity changes before interpreting drop-off.
Compare relevant segments or cohorts without treating small samples as reliable differences.
Investigate a drop-off with user feedback and propose a change addressing the observed difficulty.

levels.name: Evaluate a Product Hypothesis
levels.description: Defines and evaluates a hypothesis for an actual product change. Selects an outcome metric and guardrails before release, establishes a baseline, and interprets evidence in the context of traffic, seasonality, and qualitative observations. Uses a method that fits the project’s scale rather than requiring an A/B test for every question.
examples: Write a hypothesis linking a proposed change to a user problem, an expected behavior change, and an evaluation decision.
Define the target population, metric denominator, observation window, and relevant guardrails before collecting results.
Evaluate a released change with the available evidence and explicitly distinguish association from causal attribution.
For low traffic, combine observed task completion and user interviews and state the limits of the conclusion.

levels.name: Reliable Measurement and Controlled Experiments
levels.description: Maintains trustworthy product measurement across evolving features and runs more demanding evaluations. Where traffic and the decision justify it, applies controlled experiments with appropriate assignment, exposure tracking, sample planning, and uncertainty analysis. Uses cohort and retention analysis to avoid mistaking short-term activity for durable value.
examples: Define activation and retention around the product’s actual use cycle and compare cohorts with consistent definitions.
Version or migrate a changed event schema and verify continuity or explicitly mark a break in the metric series.
Run an appropriately scoped randomized experiment when feasible, checking assignment balance, exposure, guardrails, and uncertainty.
For an infeasible experiment, document why and execute an alternative evaluation with explicit attribution limits.
Investigate an apparent improvement for instrumentation errors, population shifts, novelty effects, or other plausible explanations.

levels.name: Sustained Evidence-Based Product Decisions
levels.description: Maintains a product measurement approach that supports important decisions over time. Connects metrics to user value and business or service goals, reviews data quality and access, and learns across multiple changes. Makes uncertainty visible and revises decisions when later evidence contradicts an initial result.
examples: Use several completed evaluations to make and follow through on a roadmap or feature-retirement decision.
Review whether the chosen product metrics still reflect meaningful user outcomes and revise misleading incentives or proxy metrics.
Maintain event ownership, quality checks, retention, and access rules as the product and team change.
Document an evaluation that led to a revised or reversed decision and explain what new evidence changed the conclusion.
Help another contributor design and interpret a product evaluation with appropriate metrics, guardrails, and honest uncertainty.
